maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.

speechtext: Mr. TURRIFF moved the second reading of Bill (No. 30) respecting the subsidy from the Ontario government to Lake Superior branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: This is a Bill to confirm an agreement made between the Ontario government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and contained in chapter 18 of the Ontario statutes of 1904. Section 21 of that Act provides that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company shall come before this parliament and get an Act to confirm the agreement. This Bill is introduced at the request of the Ontario government and to carry out that arrangement. It applies particularly to sections 3 and 22 of the Ontario Act.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: What is section 3?

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
It is as follows:
1.	In addition to the provisions of the Railway Act with respect to tolls, to be taken or levied by the said companies it is hereby enacted that there shall be no secret special rates, rebates, drawbacks or concessions to favoured shippers nor any act or thing that will affect or prevent free competition in any line or lines of trade.
2.	Each of the said companies shall be obliged, upon the request of any township or county, municipality through which the line of railway passes, to carry road making material, gravel or stone, required for improving any of the road within any such municipality, at the cost of handling and carriage.
Section 22 provides that in the event of the Dominion government taking over the road, the subsidy given by the Ontario government shall be returned to them by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. These two clauses are being confirmed in the Bill which I am now asking to be read the second time.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I have sent copies of this Bill to the city of Port Arthur, which is interested in it, because the subsidy granted by the Ontario government was granted upon condition that the road should come to the shores of Thunder bay. I do not say that this Bill would relieve the company of that obligation, but it might do so. In my opinion the road as constructed is six or seven miles from Thunder bay.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Does the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) oppose the Bill?

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: No, I am only asking that it stand until I have an opportunity of hearing from the representatives of the city of Port Arthur. I had an interview this morning with one of the gentlemen connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and I understood from him that the Bill was to stand until the solicitor of the company came here to discuss the Bill and I desire to hear from Port Arthur. I move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: LAKE SUPERIOR BRANCH GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
This Bill seems to be a peculiar Bill. If I understand it correctly, it is to carry out an arrangement made between the Ontario government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. To begin with, I can hardly accept the policy that any other government and any company can get together and make an agreement which will commit us to pass any Act. It may be all right or it may not be all right. There may be some things in the Bill which it would be perfectly proper for us to confirm in order to protect the Ontario government against any acts that might be done by the company in default; but there is another part referring to rates which to my mind is not in accordance with our Railway Act. While one portion of the Bill insists that the Grand Trunk 33
Pacific Railway Company must not give any special rates or rebates to any person, another portion says that it must give special rates and rebates. To my mind these provisions are contradictory, and we are asked to confirm them both. The Board of Railway Commissioners having been adopted by us as the means whereby we control rates, for my part I want to adhere to that policy, and I would not wish to assent to any Act that would take the control of the rates to be charged by a company chartered by this parliament away from the Railway Commission. There may be some things in the Bill that it is necessary for us to confirm, but there are two or three things in it which at present I do not think we ought to confirm.
Motion for adjournment of debate agreed to
Mr. JAMES CONMEE (Thunder Bay and Rainy River) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 34) to incorporate the Ontario and Michigan Power Company.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to give some explanation of this Bill, as I believe it is practically the same as the Bill that was introduced last year.

I did not think it necessary to take up the time of the House in discussing the Bill before it went to the committee. I think hon. gentlemen understand the Bill fairly well. It is practically the same Bill as was introduced into the Senate last year, and practically the same as was carried in the Senate two years ago, with this difference, that in the previous Bill provision was made for the storage of water on the rivers mentioned, and in the first Bill reference was made to the Sturgeon river. All reference to that river and to storage of water upon either of the streams or the tributary waters has been removed from this Bill. The hope of the promoters was to simplify the Bill in order to remove criticism. It does not differ at all from a large number of Bills that have passed this House in recent years. I may say that the Ontario legislature has passed Bills similar in character to this, but with less safeguards. If it were necessary for me at this stage to discuss the Bill specifically, I think I could satisfy hon. gentlemen that no Bill that has come before the House within recent years has had better or more specific safeguards to protect the public interest. I would suggest that the Bill be allowed to go to the committee, where it can be discussed m all its details.

This is the third session during which we have had discussion on the



principle of this Bill. Last session my hon. friend endeavoured to secure the passage of the principle of the Bill under this name and the preceding session under another name, but in each case he has met with a reverse, either in the Senate or in this House. The first Bill was defeated in this House, while the second was thrown out in the Senate committee after a somewhat lengthy debate. The objections to this Bill are serious, and I do not want to have it thought I am endeavouring captiously to take up time. By the Bill certain private rights are sought on two rivers flowing into Lake Superior, the Pigeon and Nepigon rivers. It is sought to acquire the use of the waterpower on these rivers, accompanied by the right to acquire such lands, privileges, &e., as are necessary to carry out the operation of those water-powers. The Ontario government has laid out with considerable care a power policy for the development and control of power and the regulation of rates in that province. That power policy has been twice approved by the people of Ontario. It involves the very principles of control over water-powers of which this Bill endeavours to rob the province. Therefore, if this Bill were objectionable in nothing more than its invasion and violation of the principles of provincial rights, it should not be allowed to receive its second reading. I would point out in this connection the provisions of section 14, which are as follows :
In case of any dispute or difference as to the price to be charged for power or electrical or other energy, for any of the purposes in this Act mentioned, in use or to be provided for use upon the Canadian side of the international boundary, or as to the methods of distribution thereof, or as to the time within which or as to the quantity to be furnished, or the conditions upon which they shall be furnished for use, or as to the value of any lands, timber or other material, or the exercise of any of the provisions of this Act, such dispute or difference shall, notwithstanding the provisions of section 17 of The Railway Act, be) settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada on the application of any user of or applicant fori power, electrical or other energy produoed by the Company, or upon the application of the Company.
One of the chief provisions of the Ontario Power Act is the control with regard to the user of the power and the regulation of rights which this section 14 would take away from the province. I do not want to discuss the Bill clause by clause; I am merely pointing out objections to its principle. The Senate committee was very emphatic in its condemnation of the Bill owing to its invasion of the rights of the province, counsel for the province being present and objecting to it. I hope, therefore, the House will not allow the Bill to receive its second reading.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: I would not for a moment take the ground my hon. friend does that it would be wise to negative the motion for the second reading. For my own information I would ask if these streams are boundary waters?

The Pigeon river is an international water and the Ninigon is a navigable water, and in my opinion also international in character because it forms a source of the lakes and connecting channels which are international. A case arose which makes that point quite clear in connection with the Rainy river. A company developing a power at Duluth undertook to divert a portion of the waters from the watershed of the Rainy river to the St. Louis river. The Canadian section of the Waterways Commission objected to that proceeding. There is a report upon that subject, the result of which was the Duluth Company were prevented from diverting portions of the water from flowing into Rainy lake, the source of Rainy river. The same conditions exist at Nipigon. Certain of the waters flowing into the Nipigon can be diverted very easily-I am speaking from personal knowledge of the ground-to the Albany river. There are very few points at the head of most of the large rivers on the north shore where that cannot be done, and there is a question as to where the line should be drawn as to what is international and what is not. These streams certainly form the international waters of the great lakes, and if we read correctly in the press, the recent treaty provides that the jurisdiction of the commission shall extend not only to the basin of the lakes but to the area of drainage. It is quite apparent that there must be a regulating power somewhere. In some respects the question of international waters are just as much an issue in the one stream as in the other.
Does the hon. member base his claim in reference to the Nipigon river on its being an international water?
Not at all, that is only incidental; it is a navigable water.
For what distance?

No dam or bridge can be constructed across any navigable stream without the consent of the federal authority. There is a case in point. A Bill has been passed by this House relating to the development of water-power at Fort Frances by the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company.
That is an international water.	[DOT]
Certainly, so is the Nipigon river, to a certain extent at least, in my opinion.
Not seriously?
Yes, I am quite serious, and I am quite prepared to back up my opinion with sufficient evidence.
On what do you base it?
On common sense.
Let us have a chunk of it

I know my hon. friend would perhaps be the better of a little of it. I was trying to enlighten him, if I could. I won't say at this stage that I will undertake to satisfy my hon. friend that I am right, but if he will tell me where he can draw the line between what is international and what is not international water, he will give me some information that I would like to get. The Pigeon river is an international boundary,-there can be no doubt about that.
For what distance is it an international boundary?
Perhaps three hundred miles.
Oh, no. Do you include the lakes?

Yes, the Pigeon river and the lakes in that water route extend from Lake Superior to the north west angle of the Lake of the Woods, a distance of nearly three hundred miles. If I understand correctly the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite, the question of jurisdiction would be a fair subject for legislation. I have read some newspaper articles in which it is declared that there is no more right in this parliament to grant a charter to deal with an international stream than there is to deal with any navigable stream. Perhaps some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side will enlighten us upon that point. I was referring to the Bill that passed this House in connection with the Rainy River Development Company-the Ontario and Minnesota Power Bill. That Bill did not afford sufficient protection to the public. Local interests petitioned parliament for and obtained sweeping amendments to the Bill providing for the distribution of electricity, for the outflow of the water through the waste weirs, for the establishment of the works on the Canadian side of the international boundary,-for if these waste weirs were not on the Canadian side of the boundary how could this government control the flow of the water? and how could navigation be protected below the dam if the company could hold back the waters for a week, or, as they might do, for months? For the area of Rainy lake is very great, and it would take a long time to raise its level greatly even though all the water were held back. By exercising this power, the
33i
company could destroy navigation on the river below. I do not need to argue that (question very much. But it is to the interest of a power company to hold back the flow of water until the period of low water, and then to draw the level down gradually so as to maintain their power at their power station. The result of this policy might be to make a difference of twelve or fifteen feet in the level of the lake-I am speaking of Rainy lake. I have seen differences in the level of that lake varying from six to twelve feet, the result merely of natural conditions, the precipitation and the nature of the season. These are matters that must sooner or later be provided for and dealt with by some authority; and I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they think the provincial authority has power to regulate it. I believe it has not, for it has no power over navigable waters. It is .said that because the province owns the land over which the waters flow they have paramount control.

May I ask a question? Does the hon. gentleman contend that if, in a river three hundred miles long, there is a portion fifty miles long that is navigable, therefore the Dominion has control over the whole stream?
It certainly has control over that portion that is navigable. I am not going to draw so fine a line as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) has in his mind.
This Bill takes over the whole stream.

No, but one point on the stream. In my opinion ' navigable stream ' means not only the river itself, but also the tributaries back to the watershed of the river. For, if that were not the case, it would be an easy matter to dry up the stream. I can give the hon. gentleman a case in point. In the United States the control of navigable waters is in the Secretary of War,-as these waters may be needed for purposes of defence, they are put in control of that department. The Fox river, in Wisconsin, which is the outlet of Lake Winnebago, enters Lake Michigan at Green bay. It is in about a similar position to the Nipigon. The distance from the mouth to the source of the Fox river is 45 miles. There are established along this river at Appleton, combined locks and at other points, some of the largest pulp and paper manufacturing industries in the United States. These power companies, in order to secure water for their works, had control of the lake by a dam. They drew the water down to such a level as to destroy navigation. The wharfs at the villages along the lake shore could not be reached by boat because of the low water. The federal

authorities of the United States closed the outflow, and compelled these companies to maintain the lake at mean level. It is as inevitable as anything can be that this parliament must, some day, grapple with these questions. But these questions are not raised in this Bill. The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) says that this Bill was defeated in this House. That is not the case.
He said it was defeated in the Senate.

He said it was defeated in this House too. It passed the Senate two years ago, but did not come to a vote in this House. And the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) knows very well the reason why it did not come to a vote- he obstructed it, and so the Bill was not reached. This is a very much improved Bill. I said that I did not propose to discuss the Bill on thi3 occasion. But I am willing to discuss it, and seeing that discussion is forced upon me, I will say a few words concerning it. I would ask hon. members, what is there in this Bill that interferes with provincial rights? I ask the hon. member who has already spoken and others who are yet to speak to answer that question.

Perhaps I may be permitted to say a word at this point. Suppose that on a certain stream, three hundred miles long, there is navigable water for a distance of fifty miles, and that on the rest of the stream there are many available water-powers. Now, these water-powers are regarded by the province as their asset,, and they propose to work them and control them. This Bill interferes with that right.

The hon. member, (Mr. Sproule) is entirely mistaken. The Bill takes away no rights from the province. The river is not three hundred miles long, but about forty-five miles long, and it is navigable throughout its length except at the several falls. If my recollection is correct, there is a total fall of over three hundred feet on the river, and there are seven or eight points at which about 25,000 horse power can be developed. This Bill asks for but one. Hon. gentlemen must bear in mind that it is not in the nature of a monopoly. It has been so represented, and I fear, notwithstanding the explanation of the fact, it will be still misrepresented. But there are seven or eight other points on the river at which an equal amount of power can be developed, that is, the same volume of water and the same head can be obtained at different points. This Bill asks for one. Now I may ask, does the province own the stream? I am told by very eminent legal men that there is no ownership in water, and that if there is in this case, it Mr. CONMEE.
certainly does not belong to the province. As I stated a moment ago, it is more or less international in character, because it is a feeder of these international waters that divide the two countries; there can be no question about that. The Bill merely gives this company power to go on and construct works. If the province of Ontario own any land, any rights, if they own a water privilege, why, they must be paid for it; it cannot be taken for nothing; they will have to be dealt with and their rights satisfied.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the Ontario government to-day is claiming jurisdiction over this very river, the Nipigon river, under its power law?
I am aware that the province of Ontario is objecting to all these Bills. They have an agent here and have had for the last four or five years, yet the Bills have gone through just the same.
Not this one.
They had an agent here objecting to this Bill.
But it did'nt go through.

There are good reasons why the Bill did not go through. The hon. gentleman stated that it met defeat in this House. That is not true. It did not meet defeat. The hon. member from the Soo, speaking at first, said the Bill was defeated in this House.
It did not get through thi9 House.
The hon. gentleman said it met with defeat here. He is not correct, it was not reached.
I was correct in saying that it -was defeated by the Senate committee, am I not, this same Bill?

It was defeated by the Senate committee last year. There are several reasons why the promoters of this Bill are within their rights in coming to this parliament to ask for this legislation. In the first place, they say that the legislature of Ontario has no constitutional authority to clothe them with the powers they require. The British North America Act,
I think, bears that out. Under section 92, reference is made to the exclusive powers that the legislature can exercise, and one of them is subsection 11 to charter companies for purely local objects, local enterprises confined within the province. Then, section 91 defines what subjects are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal parliament. It includes the navigation of navigable waters, railways, telegraphs, and that class of legislation. It includes other things-but I do not want to take up the time of the House by reading them, because

I assume that hon. gentlemen are fairly familiar with the Act. It includes all questions not specifically assigned to the legislatures. Now perhaps some hon. gentleman will point out where, in the constitution, there is any power assigned to the legislature of Ontario or any other legislature to confer on companies the powers which this company require to carry out their undertaking. I cannot find it, I do not think it is there. I am well aware that it may be argued that certain powers do follow; but it can be argued with a great deal more force that a company seeking powers having other than provincial objects have a right to come to this parliament, and this parliament alone can give them power to carry out their undertaking. I am fortified in that. When the Minnesota and Ontario Bill relating to the Rainy river came before this House, His Honour Judge Fitzpatrick, was then Minister of Justice. That question came before him, and he wrote a letter to the then Minister of Public Works stating his opinion that this parliament had a right to grant the legislation. His opinion went a great deal farther; I have not got it under my hand at the moment, because I did not expect to discuss this question. But it went this far. Certain amendments were proposed, to the Bill, by a petition on behalf of the town of Fort Francis, and the minister's opinion went so far as to say that in granting legislation, or in certifying to plans, the parliament of Canada had ai right to impose the conditions asked, or such of them as were in the public interest, some ten or twelve amendments were made to the Bill, as 1 have already pointed out, guarding the public interest in that respect. Then I may say that the present Minister of Justice wrote a letter last year upon this very matter; it was read, and is on record before the Senate committee, in which he stated that as the objects of this company were not confined to provincial purposes only but were also international and interprovincial, the parliament of Canada was the only power that could give them the charter they were asking for. So under these circumstances I do not think it should be treated lightly. If the interest of the public is going to be prejudiced, if the interest of Ontario is going to. be prejudiced in any sense, I could understand it, but that is not the case.

On what ground was it that the Senate rejected the Bill last
year?

That is a pretty difficult question for me to answer. In the first place, I would answer it in this way, that some of the senators did not take the trouble to understand the Bill, some of them were absent, some of them had the opinion which, I fear, some hon. gentlemen opposite entertain, or profess to entertain. I see my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) shaking his head, and I think he may hold the opinion I am about to mention, namely, that this Bill is an invasion of provincial rights. Now I take issue with that opinion. I need not refer to the British North America Act to establish the fact that this parliament has the right to pass any legislation that, in its opinion, is necessary for the order and good government of Canada, or to pass any legislation it may choose to pass that is for the general advantage of Canada. I have the section under my hand, but I will not take up the time of the House to read it. It is| admitted that they have the power. I do not think that any hon. gentleman will deny that. The constitution specifically confers upon this parliament the power to pass this legislation, it has the constitutional right to deal with the subject and the legislature has not the right to deal with it. No where in the constitution is there a specific provision that would give the legislature that power.
Is there anything in the Bill which gives the company the power to expropriate?
Yes, the company will have the power to expropriate certain lands.
No.

Let me just explain that for a moment. In other provinces this company would have the right to build these works without coming here for this right, but in Ontario land sold under the Mining Act is subject to a provision which reserves a chain as a road allowance. Along the margin of rivers, where municipalities are organized, these roads pass under the control of the municipality and become highways. In this case there' is no municipality. Therefore, the control of that chain reserve is in the Ontario government, and it is to overcome that difficulty that powers of expropriation are necessary. There is also the question of the bed of the river.
Have we the right to give the power to expropriate from the Crown in the province?

The hon. gentleman has been a member of this House for the last twenty-five years or more, and hardly a session has passed but what he has voted for granting just that power. He has conferred it upon company after company all his life, and now he is asking me a question. He had better look at his own record first. I answer: Yes, we have the right. I go further and say it is our duty to do so because it is a public enterprise. The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) asks

me if I am not aware that the Ontario government has a policy

No, I asked if they did not apply that policy to the Nipigon river and the hon. gentleman said :	Yes, they
did.
Well, I will take it that way; so far they have not applied their policy to the Nipigon river.
They claim to have applied it, but there is no power developed there.

I can put the hon. gentleman right. Some three years ago the city of Port Arthur requested the Ontario government to give them the use of 3,000 horse-power. They could have taken it from the Nipigon river, the Kaministiquia river, the Pigeon river, the Mackenzie river or a dozen other rivers, but they did not do it. Now, it has taken the Ontario government about six years to make up their minds that they are going to do something at Niagara. I am not now discussing their policy; I am not objecting to it, nor am I approving of it, but if there is any excuse for it, any justification, it is that they were going to do something with that power. I would ask the hon. gentleman how long it would be before they could spread that policy to other sections of the country. The company own the land on both sides of the river. In the case of Pigeon river, the land has long since passed from the Crown. Nevertheless the Crown may have rights in it. There was no chain reserve because the lands were patented previous to the provisions in the Ontario law. Nevertheless, the Ontario government may be said to have an interest. I believe they have. I am not disputing that. Maybe they have an interest in the bed of the river, but it is not an interest that is paramount; it is subject to the control of the Federal authority. I do not think that will be disputed. With respect to the Nipigon, or any navigable river, this parliament has the right to charter a company to improve navigation, to build dams, to build channels, to divert the water over the foreshore, to do anything of the kind, or it might go on and do it itself, and it has done it time and again. Where is there an invasion of provincial rights? These questions were not raised, I presume, in former years. It might be that the value of such undertakings was not as well understood in those days. If the province has rights we cannot take them away. There is no power in this parliament to take from the province that which it possesses. This Bill does not propose to take anything from the government or any individual. The company must first pay for what they get, so that I do not think the Mr. CONMEE.
province is in any way injured. I noted an article in the ' World ' newspaper and another in the 'Globe', in which it was urged that the measure was depriving the province of revenue. I cannot see that. If the province has any rights there it can exact a sum of money for them, it can exact an annual rent for them, or it can protect itself by getting the value of that which it possesses whether it be an easement, or whether it be a title to the land itself. It is just recently the vessel men have called the attention of the government to the fact of the interference with navigation by power companies on navigable streams. I presume that they refer principally to the Niagara river. That fact illustrates my contention that the question is one that must be dealt with in this parliament and that it must be dealt with in some authoritative way. I have read statements of what are said to be the terms of the treaty recently entered into or about to be entered into, and I was discussing it to-day with a member of the Waterways Commission. His understanding of it is that it extends to the watersheds, not alone to the basin of the lakes but to the source of the lakes. I take it for granted that that would be a necessary condition, and I understand that the treaty makes provision for that. So that, we have this question to deal with. Now, I submit that no good purpose can be served by holding the Bill back to be discussed in this House. The best plan is to let the Bill go to the committee. There is nothing in the Bill which is not in lots of other Bills. The Bill is subject as well to amendment. I may say to hon. gentlemen on behalf of those for whom I am acting that I shall fight as hard as I can for the principle of the Bill. If defeated, we will take defeat, but we must be defeated fairly. The Bill has never been discussed on its merits in this House or ever in committee, and I do not want hon. gentlemen to assume that because I have referred to the Bill to-day that in the rambling remarks which I have made, I have grappled with the questions or discussed them in all the fulness with which they should be discussed. I do trust that hon. gentlemen will allow the Bill to go to committee and then we will get at it in the regular way.

I do not intend to discuss the principle of the Bill now, but in justification of a statement I made with reference to it I have to offer a few remarks. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) is applying for a charter to utilize the waters of the Nipigon river, not for navigation purposes, but for power purposes, and he tells us the Nipigon is an international river between Ontario and the United States. What right has this House to give any company the right to dam a

navigable river for the purpose of utilizing its water-power? That river is navigable form Lake Superior to Lake Nipigon, and I remember that the hon. gentleman himself had a measure before us the object of which was to navigate that river and in connection with a rail haul to carry freight for the building of the Transcontinental Railway. I asked the hon. gentleman did he ask for powers of expropriation and he expressed much surprise that I should ask such a question. I ventured mildly to say that we were not in the habit of giving expropriation powers to private companies and he retorted that I ought to know better. I can tell him that we never do give such powers to any company that is not declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.
This Bill declares that it is for the general advantage of Canada.

If it does, then that is still more objectionable. If by merely declaring a work for the general advantage of Canada that is all that is necessary to give a private company power to utilize the waters of a boundary river and to expropriate property belonging to the Crown in Ontario, it is time there was an end put to that kind of thing. These local companies with local objects should go to the provinces for their power. Why, if all you have to do is to say in a Bill that it is for the general advantage of Canada, you might over-ride every provincial right. Surely some reason must be given to show that such a work is for the general benefit of Canada beyond our mere ipse dixit in an Act of this parliament.

As one of the young members of this House, I find it somewhat difficult to follow the legislation which is brought before us. This Bill has only come to my attention within the last few moments, and while I shall not refer now to the interference with provincial rights which may be involved, yet I see another principle incorporated in this Bill which as a young Canadian I strongly object to. My objection is not so much to what this Bill says as to what it does not say. I hold the belief, Sir, that the water system of this country is the most valuable asset we have, and I asume that the water-power which this Bill seeks to monopolize belongs to the people of Canada. We had a gentleman of some eminence in this city a few days ago and he told us that the future of the American continent was dependent upon its water-powers, and to that question I shall briefly allude now. Section 13 of this Bill provides that this company shall at all times be prepared to furnish for use in Canada one-half the water-power it develops. Here we are, a people of about 7,000,000 adjoining a nation of nearly 100,000,000 with immense means to develop international waters for power purposes, while we are not in a position at present to keep pace with them in that respect. I object to the principle of allowing power to be sent out of this country to develop another country, until at all events we know that we have power sufficient for the purposes of Canada for all time to come. If hon. gentlemen opposite can assure me of that, then I would not be selfish about it, but I do not want to see this country put in the position that in the future we will have fifty per cent of our power exported to the United States, while lacking sufficient for uttr own purposes. Vested interests will be created on the other side and trouble will come if, once having allowed its export, we should attempt to keep our own power in our own country for our own development. I feel strongly about this matter and I regret that I had not the opportunity to go more fully into the Bill. But I thought I should present these views so that I might ask the House to proceed cautiously with legislation of this character.

I entirely support what has been said by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath). The hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) has made out a very good case why this Bill should be thrown out. Something may be said to support the contention that the Pigeon river is an international river, but any gentleman who will stand up in this House and in cold blood argue that the Nipigon river is an international stream ought to be laughed out of court. The Nipigon river is entirely within the province of Ontario, and whether it is a navigable stream or not is another question, but for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) to ask us to declare that the Nipigon river is an international river is asking us to swallow too much. The hon. member (Mr. Conmee) has told us that we have in this parliament passed many charters similar to the one he now asks for, but surely we ought to learn wisdom as the years go by, and if we have passed legislation containing any improvident provisions, that is no reason why we should continue in our wrong-doing. We are only now beginning to learn the real value of our water-powers in Canada; we are told that water is to be our coal in the future, and that being so we should safeguard this natural asset in every way. To pass a Bill with such sweeping provisions as this, allowing these private individuals to expropriate property from the province of Ontario and to control the water in two of the great streams of that province, would be a huge mistake.
This Bill was thrown out in the Senate last year, and I assume that there was good reason for that. At all events, it seems, to me that we ought not to give it even a

second reading when on, its face it claims to relate to a work for the general advantage of Canada. That language is absurd, as it relates to a purely local undertaking. The hon. member for Rainy River has challenged us on this side of the House to point out in the British North America Act where power is given to the local legislature to grant a charter of this nature. One would suppose that the hon. member had been studying the British North America Act night and day, and had it by heart; but I find no difficulty in pointing to a clause in the British North America Act giving the Ontario legislature power to deal with this matter. Subsection 10 of section 92 mentions, among the other powers of the local legislatures, that with reference to ' local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes; ' and these exceptions are limited to ' those which connect the province with another province or extend beyond the limits of the province.' In other words, the local legislature is distinctly given power over works such as are proposed on the Nipigon river. At all events, I for one would certainly be opposed to this Bill getting even a second reading, while it has section 2 in it.

This is a discussion of a very old subject. I think it was at the last session that a very lengthy discussion arose with respect to a Bill entitled ' An Act to incorporate the Saskatchewan Power Company.' I raised the question on that occasion of not so much the power but the advisability of this parliament attempting to deal with the subject. I deprecated the idea of the parliament of Canada incorporating companies which might properly be incorporated by the legislatures of the respective provinces, and I think it was pointed out that any company seeking such powers could secure them from the provincial legislature. The necessary powers in connection with the damming of streams or the construction of other works on streams or the control of water would necessarily be obtained from the Minister of Public Works, to whom this parliament has in a measure delegated these powers by the Act relating to Public Works and navigable waters; so that a company securing from the provincial legislature power to build dams and construct other works could only do so after obtaining permission from the Minister of Public Works. The Act incorporating the Saskatchewan Power Company was passed last session, and the strange feature of that Act was that there was no declaration in it that the work was to be one for the general advantage ot Canada. Moreover, we gave the company power to expropriate land, on the ground that the Dominion government owned the lands in the western provinces, and controlled the navi-Mr. PERLEY.
gation of the Saskatchewan river. Now, it seems to me that if this parliament was justified in incorporating the Saskatchewan Power Company, it is much more justified in incorporating this company, inasmuch as it relates to an international stream.
Mr. Sproule. The Nipigon river is not an international stream, though the Pigeon river is; but they seek power to deal with both.

So far as the Bill relates to an international stream, the power should be sought from this parliament; and I go further and say that the provincial legislature would have no power to deal with it. Therefore the object of this Bill carries with it the implication that this parliament must deal with this subject, and that the promoters of the legislation could not secure the necessary power from the local legislature. We did not refuse to send to the committee the Bill to incorporate the Saskatchewan Power Company, and I think it would be fair to send this Bill to the committee. There the provisions of the several sections could be dealt with, and those which properly come under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature could be removed from the Bill.

I listened very attentively to the remarks made by the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), and one of the reasons he advanced in appealing to the House to allow the second reading of the Bill, was of such a startling nature that the House had better be careful of the legislation on which it is entering. He gave as a reason that one, of these rivers, while not itself on the international boundary, flowed into one of the great lakes, and therefore became an international stream.

If the hon. member will pardon me, I did not make that statement. I stated that because it was a tributary of the great lakes, as the question of the right of international waters extended to the watershed, it more or less became a question in issue in this case in regard to that river. I did not go beyond that point.

The hon. gentleman has gone a good deal farther than I stated, for he would not only include such a stream as that, but all other streams which might flow into it. It is very easy to lay this down as an abstract principle, but when one lays aside the superlative wisdom which only would justify a man in moving the second reading of a Bill like this, and. comes down to ordinary everyday life and thinks applying the principle to our own province, say to the city of Toronto, we would find that the Humber and the Don were two international streams, and that it would be necessary for this parliament

to legislate in regard to any works that might be proposed to be constructed on those two rivers. The hon. gentleman seems to be so consumed with the importance of those works which are stated to be for the general advantage of Canada that they have obscured his vision altogether and he cannot see that they are not for the general advantage of the country.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that this government has exercised power with regards to the works on the Don?

Very possible under certain circumstances it might, but I do not think it has ever laid down that it would be proper for this government to give a company power to construct a dam 10 to 15 miles up the Don on account of its being an international stream and the dam being for the general advantage of Canada.
I do not think that the House has up to the present time gone as far as that. Not only is there the objection to the principle laid down, but there is a very strong objection to allowing a Bill to go to its second reading with this objectionable clause in it.
I venture to say that when the British North America Act was passed it never entered into the contemplation of the legislators of the old country who framed section 92 (10-C):
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
That this clause was intended to be other than such a clause would be in the case of a parliament similar to that which passed the British North America Act; it was taken for granted that there would at least be some conscience in a parliament dealing with these questions. It was never contemplated that the Dominion parliament would declare the most contemptible, insignificant, little piece of work to be for the general advantage of Canada. It was never expected that this House would declare something that was obviously untrue, and thereby bring such little pieces of work within its jurisdiction. I have no hesitation in saying that this House would be departing entirely from the principles of good government if it allowed the passage of such a Bill. I suppose the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) thought he had simply to insert the second clause declaring this to be for the general advantage of Canada and every member of this House, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, would leap to his feet to secure this valuable work which would contribute so much to the happiness and prosperity of his constituents. When we come to deal with it in the spirit of common sense I do not think the hon. gentleman himself would advance any particular reason why this paltry enterprise should be declared for the general advantage of Canada. If the clause stated that it was for the general disadvantage of Canada I could understand it being inserted in the Bill. One has only to look at the clause allowing the rivers to be dammed and consider what the hon. gentleman says about one river being navigable and the other international to see that it is an imposition on the common sense and good nature of this House to ask for the passage of the Bill'.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Quite apart from the question of the general advantage of Canada is it the hon. gentleman's opinion that under the constitution, by which navigable rivers are placed under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, such a river could be barred or impeded in any way by an Act of a local legislature; in other words, that the local legislature can give authority to bar or impede a navigable river?

I certainly think not;
I think the local legislature would not have power to give a company authority to bar the navigation of a navigable river, but at the same time I think if the water-power were sufficient to justify works being constructed, the local legislature of Ontario could do as they have done at Niagara and give power to a company to extract power from the water, although not the power to dam the river.
Mr. Speaker
Mr. Speaker
I allowed the hon. member for Rainy River to speak the second time in answer to a question.

I think I have the permission of the hon. member who had the floor. I wanted to answer one or two ques tions. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Magrath) stated that he was opposed to granting permission to export a portion of this power into the United States. That is the general law. The power at Niagara has been exported for many years. We have an Act of parliament governing it, and that clause was put in as a protection so that half the power might be always at the demand of the Canadian people. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) calls this an insignificant piece of work. It is a work involving the development of 35,000 or 40,000 horse-power. It is proposed to extend the lines into various parts of Canada as well as to the United States, and yet the hon. gentleman chooses to sneer at it
I do not think I can allow the hon. gentleman to proceed on this line.

introduced which, without that declaration, would obviously be within the power of the provincial legislature alone, and have asked the parliament of Canada, without investigation, and without any clear right or authority, to pass these measures and in that way assume jurisdiction over the matters in question. That ought to be corrected. It has, in the past, led to the invasion of provincial rights and of the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. I believe that no such declaration ought to be made by the parliament of Canada, except after the most careful investigation, at which the provincial authorities should have the right to be heard; and it should be made only in cases where it is perfectly clear that the undertakings are really for the general advantage of Canada. In what respect should this undertaking be declared to be ' for the general advantage of Canada ' ? How will it advantage the province of British Columbia, or the province of Prince Edward Island, that this particular water-power should be developed on the Nipigon river ? Such an undertaking is obviously not within the class contemplated by the provisions of the British North America Act to which I have called attention. So far as jurisdiction is concerned, it does not seem to me that my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) has made good his case, with respect to the Nipigon river at least. Over and over again, we have seen instances in this parliament of men coming to parliament with particular undertakings in their minds, affixed to these undertakings being something else which is really within the jurisdiction of this parliament of Canada although the main part of the undertaking is not within our jurisdiction. Whether that is the case in this instance or not I do not know. But in every case where there is suspicion that this is being done, parliament should give the most careful attention to the undertaking and should see to it that parliament is not imposed upon by constructive fraud of that kind.
As to the expediency of passing the legislation, I wholly concur in the cogent observation of my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath). Mr. Gifford Pinchot, in his very illuminating and instructive address delivered in Ottawa not long ago, pointed out that the astutest and most far-sighted men in the United States, possessing wealth and influence, are already seizing upon the water-powers of the United States with an eye to the conditions that will exist twenty-five, fifty, or a hundred years hence. Why should we not look to the same conditions that are likely to obtain in the future in this great country? Why should we enable any man, or set of men, to create in this country the beginning of a monopoly in respect of matters of this kind? As mv hon. friend (Mr. Magrath) has well said, these water-powers will be of infinitely great-

er importance twenty-five years hence thau they are to-day, and they ought to be preserved and retained, as far as possible, for the benefit of the people of the whole country, and not given away for the purpose of creating ten, fifteen, or twenty millionaires of the future. As to this question of expendi-ency, I am ready to concede that we cannot well debate it now. If parliament is to be assumed to have the jurisdiction, the matter of expediency can best be considered in committee. If it does go to committee and if the committee is called upon to consider it in that aspect, then I think very careful attention should be given to the observations of my hon. friend from Medicine Hat, as well as to those of my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr.Perley), and we should have good reasons indeed from the promoters to justify us in passing such legislation as this, which confers upon them that which, though nominally not so, may become, in substance, a monopoly.
Hon.. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals). The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has put the vital points in the proposition now before the House. One is: Have we the right to pass this legislation? The second is: Granted that we have the right to pass this legislation, ought we to pass it? Of course, it is conceded that a great many things that men as well as parliaments have the right to do may wisely be left undone. I am not saying that that is the case here, but it is a point for the House to consider. The question of provincial rights is one that is now before the public, and will be so long as we are a community divided into provincial and federal jurisdictions. I have always endeavoured very carefully to protect the rights of the provinces in their spheres, and I am prepared to continue to do so. On the other hand we must not be so careful about protecting the rights of others that we give up rights of our own. The line of demarcation is sometimes difficult to draw when you come to a question of this kind. Here we find one stream, an international one. and another one in respect of which the point raised is navigation. I will not discuss the question of expediency, because, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) says, we can better discuss it in committee. This much, however, might, in fairness, be pointed out in reply to my hon. friend, and in support of a measure, it is debatable whether it is wise to refrain in all cases from developing a power merely because part of the energy developed will have to be exported. It may be that the demand in Canada, at present, is not sufficient to warrant capital in developing the power at all. Would it be wise to allow Canada to remain for years without her share in that development, or would it be better to allow it to be developed so that Canada could get the share that she can use leaving the remainder to be exported? It is a fine point to argue. I think that, in some circumstances, we would be warranted, in order to secure the development ourselves, to allow part of the power to be exported, if the denial of this right would mean that we could not get capital sufficient to develop the power. Then there is the question my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) has brought up, and which has been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. It is well known that this question of our water-powers, the preservation of our forests and reforestation are live questions, and they are so interlinked with one another that you can hardly discuss one without dealing with the others. The denuding of our forest areas means the destruction of our water-powers; and this question is of such magnitude that, as hon. members are aware, a conference is being opened in Washington this week in which the United States, Mexico, and Canada are taking part for the discussion of the general subject of conserving our natural resources, including these which we have been discussing to-day. I earnestly hope that something will develop from that conference that will give us some light in dealing with tnese matters; because if there is one thing more than another that means a great deal to the Dominion of Canada at the present time,
I think it is this question of water as a transportation medium, and water as a power developer. These two things are of vast importance to Canada, and to conserve them as far as possible for our own benefit I think ought to be the study of all men who take an active part in public life.
Now the Bill before us raises, as I have said, the question of provincial rights to a certain extent. I am not sure just to what extent it is raised. I have listened with a good deal of attention to my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), and the way he has put his case. If the paragraphs m the Bill contain bona fide statements, then it becomes an international work and ought to be dealt with by this House; and if it be truly an international work it could not be dealt with by any other power than this House. My hon. friend has referred to the innocent yet powerful paragraph saying that this work is for the general advantage of Canada. I am afraid-and I am comparatively free to say so, and can afford to criticise-I am afraid that this parliament perhaps for many years gone by has been quite a sinner in that regard. Looking at this question from the standpoint I have occupied for the last eight or ten years- excepting the last two years-I have often thought these words were placed in Bills when they had no right to be there, and that charters were issued to railway companies and other companies by Dominion authority that should have been left to provincial authorities. My view point has not changed in that respect. I believe that

there is a sphere which truly belongs to the provinces and which we should not interfere with; on the other hand, we have our own sphere that we should jealously guard. I have just been looking at it, because I hardly expected it would come up to-day- and without committing myself to this Bill at all on the second reading, there may be portions of it that ought to go through and others that ought not. As the leader of the opposition says, those representing the provincial side of the case could be best heard before the committee. With that understanding, and so as to give all parties, including the province, a right to be heard, I have no objection to the Hill being sent to the committee, reserving the right to oppose the Bill in committee, and not committing myself at the present stage to any points in the Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton).
speechtext:
I have listened with a good deal of interest to the leader of the opposition discussing this very interesting question of constitutional law, because after all the interesting parts of it are the constitutional phases which are raised. I think it is conceded that we have a right to pass a part of this Act of incorporation, and if there were no other authority for that than the statement of the hon. leader of the opposition, as a Nova Scotia man, I would be quite prepared to accept it. But I would not have said anything if the leader of the opposition had gone a little further and dealt with the question of what I would call the smaller streams. This international stream may not be the larger one, but I take it for granted that it is the larger one, and that the other streams mentioned are the smaller ones. I think the legal gentlemen of the House will agree that the law has been found to be that if this House has a right to grant a charter for the main purpose-and I think the main purpose to be to control, or to do something in the way of controlling, an international stream-if that right is in this House; if then it becomes incidental to carrying out that main purpose to grant the further power, we have the right even if, in principle, and on the face of it we have to transgress provincial rights. That statement is in accord with the decisions of the Privy Council on this point. Then if it is necessary to control this Nipigon river or other small streams, if it is necessary in order to carry out the purpose of this charter to control these small streams to expropriate land, or do anything else that may be necessary to carry out the main purpose of the company, then there is jurisdiction in this House under the decisions of the Privy Council, to grant a| charter and to extend the powers to the necessary extent. I think the legal gentle men of the House will agree with that proposition. It would appear to be largely Mr. GRAHAM.
a question whether the acquiring of these smaller streams is incidental to the main purpose or not. Now as to the general proposition, as to the ownership of the streams in the older provinces, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, where the land is vested in the provinces, I think it will be conceded that the property in the streams is in the local government, subject to rights of navigation. I think that is the law. But in Manitoba and the west generally, where the land is not vested in the provincial governments, that doctrine, of course, would require some modification. Whether it can be stated as a matter of law that the right in a stream is in the provincial government when they do not own any land at all? I am not expressing an opinion on that point.
This is in the province of Ontario entirely, except the portion that is near the international boundary.

So far as I know anything about it, I would say that so far as smaller streams are absolutely within the province of Ontario, the right to the land and the right to the bed of the river is in the provincial government, subject to rights of navigation. But as I said before, if interfering in any way with the smaller streams is necessary to the carrying out of the main purpose of this charter, then the right is in this parliament to grant and control those rights, if it is incidental to carrying out the main purpose of the character.
I did not understand that this was the case of a large stream which is an international stream, and smaller ones ancillary to it, but they are two absolutely distinct streams.

Well, that does not affect my argument. Even if it is a smaller stream, if, in order to carry out the purpose for which the charter was granted, it is necessary to have something to do with the smaller stream, the right is vested in this parliament to grant that right.
These are both large streams, and they are hundreds of miles apart.

They may be, but what I say is clear. I see the hon. member for North Toronto, who is no doubt a distinguished lawyer, laughing and shaking his head. But it has so happened that even distinguished constitutional lawyers like himself have agreed and laid down the principle which I simply reiterate, that if it is necessary to transgress provincial rights in order to carry out the main purpose of a charter which we have a right to grant, that right is vested in this House. That is a principle which I merely reiterate. It is a question of fact and not a question of law whether the acquisition of rights over these smaller

streams in the province of Ontario is incidental to the main purpose or not. If it is not incidental to the main purpose, I certainly say that I do not think there is anv jurisdiction in this House to interfere with it unless clause two of the Act is accepted.
What about the ex' ercise of a right in a case like this?

What I said is clear, I said that so far as an international stream is concerned, we have the right, that is, conceded by every lawyer in this House, and to interfere with what may be regarded as provincial rights so far as that is necessary to carry out the purpose of the main cb arter.
What about the justice of so interfering?
That is a question of fact. I do not know the facts and I am not going to state any opinion. I am dealing with the question of law.
No one disputes that we have the power.

I say we have not the power unless the interfering with the smaller streams is necessary for the carrying out of the greater project over which we have the greater right. As far as the conserving of the water power is concerned and keeping it within our jurisdiction, I agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to this extent that it is not an easy matter to say that we shall always hold this power in reserve, not touching it and looking for some future development or necessity. The government of Nova Scotia, some time ago, made a new departure in connection with the granting of lands and water-powers. They do not grant absolute rights to any person with respect to these franchises or properties. They have adopted the policy of leaseholds, and I think it would be the better policy in this case. . I do not think it is wise to grant an absolute right or power with respect to water or water-powers any more than it is wise to give absolute control oyer coal lands. In Nova Scotia we only give leaseholds for coal properties and for many years, when persons have come to the local legislature looking for powers with respect to streams,. we have adopted the course of giving them a lease subject to the absolute control of the government and subject to cancellation. In cases where the Dominion government part with control over these resources, or permit the exercise of these powers, I think a policy similar to that adopted in the province of Nova Scotia would be advisable, and in that way keep these resources under the control of the government, so that if in the future the
necessity arises for a change in the conditions such change can be made. In so far as the constitutional question is concerned, that is the view I take and I would not have said anything at all if the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) had dealt with these incidental powers which are vested in this House provided the exercise of them is essential to the main purpose of the charter.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) who is promoting the Bill, what his estimate is of the water power on the Nipigon river ? I understand him to say that it is 80,000 horse-power on the Pigeon river. What has he estimated for the Nipigon ?
It is estimated that the Nipigon river has about 200,000 horsepower. This one point would cover perhaps 20,000 or 25,000 horse-power.

The Nipigon river is 100 miles away from the Pigeon river and they have nothing whatever to do with each other. There is another matter which has not been touched upon and which ought to be mentioned. Nipigon lake and Nipigon river possess the best trout fishing in the world There should be nothing allowed to be done to interfere with this famous fishing resort. There are a great many tourists coming from New York, Boston, Philadelphia and other places to fish in Nipigon river and lake. The hon. gentleman says this is a navigable river, but he will not . say that it is continuously navigable. You can navigate it by canoes which enable you to get around the rapids, but you cannot navigate it with any other craft. You get the finest speckled trout in the world in Nipigon lake, which has a coast line almost equal to that of Lake Ontario, and I think that this House and this committee before adopting this Bill, should obtain the fullest information as to the proposal of this company and the condition of these waters. The Nipigon and Pigeon rivers nave no more to do with each other than black has with white. I think the hon. gentleman has simply hitched the two together to get them both through because the power of the Nipigon is more valuable man that of the Pigeon. He had in his Bill of last year the Sturgeon river. There is not as much power on the Sturgeon river as on the Nipigon river, but there is a good deal. I do not think that a Bill granting such wide powers should be allowed to go through this House in the interest of American capitalists. The hon. gentleman has just enough Canadians in it to give colour to it. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) presented to the House an argument in favour of the development of this power because the people

want to use it, but when there is need for the power there is no question but that capital will come in to develop it. This is a question that this House ought to consider very seriously before taking the step proposed by the hon. gentleman who has introduced this Bill. I have been up both of these rivers by canoe and I know something about them. The House knows very little about them. If this Bill is permitted to go to the committee, there should be the fullest information available with reference to maps, the location of these rivers, their navigability and the value of the water-powers upon them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the sense of the House seems to- be that this Bill should go to the committee, not permitting our own judgment to affirm the principle but simply to have the matter dealt with and investigated, both as to jurisdiction and policy. With regard to the question of jurisdiction of this House, I think, for my part, that the jurisdiction is certainly in this House and not in the local legislature. The local legislature has been jealous, and naturally so, that their powers should not be interfered with by any action of this House, and in so far as this view of theirs is concerned I would be disposed to respect it in its entirety. But, I would lay this proposition before the House: With regard to one of these schemes, suppose that this work should be necessary, that it would bo to the advantage of the public and that parliament, representing the people of Canada generally, should be of the opinion that this work should be constructed, who has the power to create the entity which brings this work into being? As to one of these streams,, the Pigeon river, everybody is agreed that the parliament of Canada alone has that power. I think there is no question as to that. That was stated by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). But, if I understood my hon. friend, a moment ago, he stated also with regard to the Nipigon river that as it is altogether situated in the province of Ontario, and that although it is a navigable river the province of Ontario would have the power to create the entity which would be necessary to be created in order to carry out the work and not this government. But, he qualified his contention by the statement that whilst the local legislature has power to create the entity, still the power which is vested in this new entity would be exercised only by coming to the Minister of Public Works and obtaining authority to deal with a navigable river.
Just as this company would be obliged to do.

hon. friend the leader of the opposition to the fact that in so far as a navigable river is concerned the local legislature has not the power to create a corporation which *would exercise any rights over a navigable stream.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I assume it is not in the power of a provincial legislature to give authority to create any work interfering with a navigable river, but power is given to the Minister of Public Works to pass regulations with respect to works which are authorized. The Minister of Public Works cannot give authority to a thing which is illegal in itself, but he supervises the exercise of the power granted by this parliament. If this parliament gives power to construct a bridge or any work over a navigable river, the authority to which this power is given must go before the Minister of Public Works to have its plans approved. I do not know that it goes any further than that and, therefore, I would assume that the authority to deal with a navigable river is left exclusively with this parliament. I do not give this as a final opinion; I simply throw it out for consideration. I am very glad this Bill will go before the committee because I am not at all sure as to the power, and on the question of policy I have very serious doubts that we should pass this Bill.

If the right hon. gentleman looks at section 3 he will see that the effect of it is that while the statute contains provisions against any interference with navigable waters it says:
Except so much of this part as relates to
rebuilding or repairing any lawful work, nothing hereinafter in this part contained shall apply to any work constructed under the authority of any Act of parliament of Canada or of the legislature of the late province of Canada, or of the legislature of any province now forming part of Canada, passed before such province became a part thereof.
That exactly lets in the exception I have referred to. For example, in the port of Halifax if any one should desire to extend his wharf so as to interfere with navigation he would apply to the Minister of Public Works for permission and he might get it.
He need not get incorporated himself.

It is not a question of incorporation at all. A private citizen owning some land bordering on the harbour and perhaps owning some land under the water may desire to improve his property by building a work which will interfere with navigation and he must get authority to do so. If he sells his land to a company incorporated by the provincial legislature and that company desires to do the same thing, it must come equally to the Department of Public Works for permission before that work can be lawfully constructed. If that permission is not obtained then the work is a public nuisance. That whole subject was gone into in a case argued before the Supreme Court of Canada about 20 years ago. A man had constructed a wharf out into the harbour of Halifax without obtaining permission and a vessel ran into it and there was negligence on one side or the other, and the wharf owner lost his case, if I remember correctly, for the reason that the wharf was a public nuisance at the time inasmuch as this permission had not been obtained. My point was simply this:	That if a company in the province
of Ontario is authorized to develop water-powers generally, without naming any river -and a river or stream need not be named -it would require to come to the Department of Public Works in respect to a navigable river and obtain permission to interfere with navigation, and, inasmuch as the Bill does not authorize interference with navigation this company would have to do the same thing. Therefore, the argument that it is navigable water falls to the ground, because the question of interference with navigable water has already been dealt with by the parliament of Canada in such a way as to enable a company whether incorporated by the provincial legislature or by the parliament of Canada to interfere with that navigation, but only under certain conditions and with the authority of the Department of Public Works.

The officials of the department who conducted the investigations inquired as to the names of the persons from whom the coal oil which exploded was purchased or obtained, the names of the firms by whom it was originally supplied, and the manner in which it was being used at the time of the explosions. Samples of the oil which exploded could not be secured, but samples of similar oil in the possession of persons from whom the oil which exploded was purchased were, in every case where possible, obtained and tested. Numerous samples of oil in the hands of different dealers and oil merchants were also tested.
The results of these investigations show that in every case (except one, which was due to the explosion of a lamp), the accidents were caused by the pouring of coal oil on smouldering fires in order to hasten the burning of the fuel; that in some instances the oil was fully up to the standard required by law, that in other instances it was below, and that it is extremely dangerous both to life and property to pour coal oil on a fire no matter how perfect the quality may be.
Two dealers who had sold coal oil which exploded, and which was not up to the standard, were prosecuted and condemned
