He said: Mr. Speaker, this is exactly the same motion that I made last year. I have several reasons why I thought it best to introduce it again this year. One was that last year it was introduced on a Wednesday afternoon and there were only four of the hon. members who were able to speak on the question, while there were some fourteen or fifteen who desired to do so. I thought it better to bring in the motion again this year in order that every one, if possible, who had nothing to say upon it last year might speak now and also that those who did speak upon it last year might have the privilege of doing so again. Another reason is that I, as well as other medical men, consider this if not the most important, one of the most important questions that could be introduced into the parliament of Canada. This question affects
not only the lives and health of our people, but the prosperity of the country. It affects the Finance Department, the Labour Department; it affects the prosperity of the country now and its future greatness. Thirdly, I introduced it again because it is the wish of the medical profession and many of the laity. In introducing this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I may say that I represent not only many laymen interested in improving the health of the people, but I represent 6,000 medical men in the Dominion of Canada. I may say that this is not my question. As you well know it is not my resolution, but it is the motion of the medical profession of Canada. I happen to be one, although at the present time, at least, disengaged from the activities that claim the energies of nearly the whole of the 6,000 medical men, and you all know the hard, busy life of the medical man. He would give greater public utterance to his views upon this question of public health had he more leisure. His time of work extends not only from morning till night, but from morning till morning sometimes, and again from morning till night without any let-up for rest. He has not only to provide for a family, for those dependent upon him, but for the welfare of innumerable sick who take the most of his thoughts and his time. For that reason we do not hear, as often as we otherwise would, the voice of the medical man on this question of public health. Nevertheless he is thinking of it; nevertheless, he is acting about it. When medical men meet in annual association, as we do for the whole Dominion once a year, and for every province once a year, and for every county sometimes as often as once a month, this question comes up very prominently. It is more before the medical profession to-day than it ever was; it is more before the public of Canada to-day than it ever was. Those of the medical men who have been reading the public addresses of presidents of medical associations, and of medical men before the Canadian clubs or other bodies throughout Canada will agree that, for the last two or three years, the burden of these addresses Ras been ' the public health.' Formerly, at the annual meeting of the medical association, some subject of disease or its treatment, some surgical operation, was usually introduced by the president in his annual address. Now, I have observed, year after year, the presidential address is on some such subject as Public Health, State Medicine or Hygiene. This subject has taken such a hold in the neighbouring republic than a committee of one hundred laymen has been working steadily for the last four or five years to induce the American government to consolidate their various federal boards of health into one single bureau of public heath. And this is the course we hope to see taken in Canada.

Such a hold has this question taken in the United States that Columbia University, one of the first universities on this continent, has taken the lead and established a chair of Public Health, the first of the kind in any medical college in the world. Heretofore medical colleges have contented themselves with teaching how to cure diseases-to the making of people well. Now, Columbia University, in the city of New York, is in the advance guard, teaching medical men how to teach the public to keep from getting sick. It is rather anomalous that we should be engaged in spoiling our own business. But there are a great many men-the great majority-in the medical profession who are willing to sacrifice themselves for the benefit of others rather than consider their own selfish profit.
Hear, hear.

Two or three laymen say,
' hear, hear.' I am glad to hear them say, it. I am now in the ranks of the older men of the medical profession; I have practised alongside two generations of them down in that province by the sea; and I would like to say that I do not believe that in any profession or business in this country, or. any other country that I have ever known, can be found a more self-sacrificng, unselfish, generous body of men than the medical men whom I have known and practised along side of. And I take them as a sample of those to be found all over Canada. I also had another reason for introducing this to-day, because, though, last year, I got a speech into the heads of) the government, I want, to-night, if it is within my power, to get it into their hearts. I want them to dream dreams and see visions of this subject, until a bureau of public health for the education and instruction of the people shall be established here I do not think we have any right to wait to see what other countries are doing. We are forming here one of the latest, and, as we hope, one of the greatest nations in the world. We are the ' heir of all the ages,' and) we can pattern by the mistakes and sins of omission and of commission of other countries. And as we are, man for man, the best educated country in the world-and I say that advisedly, and can quote one of the best authorities in Canada in support of my statement-we should lead in this question of public health for the sake of humanity.
I plead this cause of a bureau of public health for several reasons. I plead it because Canada is suffering enormous losses of people yearly from diseases that could be prevented. I plead it because we are suffering not only loss of people, but loss of enormous money values. I plead it because this loss is unnecessary-because there is no reason why it should continue.

Spend a fraction of that in educating our people how to avoid the disease and in teaching these cities which are now scattering typhoid all over Canada how to prevent typhoid, and how much of this $27,000,000 a year would be saved? I say that from a monetary point of view alone we can afford to take active and energetic measures to prevent typhoid, and we will be richer in the end for it. Is it the duty of the government to embark in this good work ? I think so. This government admits it is their duty to teach the people to conserve our natural resources and to protect out forests; they consider it their duty to protect our domestic animals from disease. This government very wisely expends half a million dollars a year and they employ 107 veterinarians to protect the lives of our domestic animals. Is not a man worth more than a sheep; is not a human being worth more than an ox ? And if it is the duty of the government to protect the lives of our domestic animals is it not one-thousand-fold more their duty to protect the lives and the health of our own people ? There is a little story told by Dr. Hurty, so short and so much to the point that I will venture to repeat it to the House.
A little mother under 25 years of age was told by her physician that she had the beginnings of consumption. She was told that it was curable, that the government had sanitoria to cure it. She wrote to the government saying:	I am
told that I have consumption in its early stages and can be cured by outdoor life, continued rest and plenty of food. I do not want to die; I want to live. I think I am of value to the State; I want to raise my children, to make them good citizens. Where can I get well?	.
The reply was to this effect: This great Christian country has not yet risen to the mighty economy cl saving the lives of its people or its little mothers from consumption or any other disease. At the present Mr. BLACK.
time, so far as we are concerned, the only place you can go to is the grave. The little mother died of consumption, that preventable, that curable disease; the home was broken up and the children were taken to the orphan asylum.
That is the first part of the story-this is the second:
A big fat hog one morning found that he had a pain in his stomach. He squealed loudly and the farmer came out of his house to see what was the matter. The hired man said :	He has got the ' hog
cholera.' So the farmer telegraphed to the Secretary of the Veterinary Department of the government, and the reply came quick:	Why certainly I will send you a
man right away. And sure enough the man came. He said he was a D.V.S.-that is, a Doctor of Veterinary Surgery, and he was, too. He had a government _ syringe and a bottle of government medicine in his hand bag; he went for the hog and the hog got well.
Now here is the moral-be a hog and be worth saving.
Mr. Speaker, if hogs can be saved, men can be saved; if it is worth the while of the government to save a hog, it is a million times more worth while to save the lives of human beings. I do want the government to get it into their heads that the lives of the people can be saved and must be saved. Of course it costs money, but is it not worth the expenditure? From a monetary point of view only, is it not worth the expenditure ? I do not want to touch upon the sentimental side of this question, although there is a sentimental side to it. There are tragedies from the ravages of disease which, if pictured in better words than I can command, would bring tears to every eye in this House. When we consider the needless loss of so many people, when we consider the enormous death rate,_ the suffering and the agony of little infants who have died from poisoned milk, we stand aghast. No medical man who has attended a case of cholera infantum, infantile diarrhoea or acute indigestion, all coming from poisoned milk-and when I say poisoned milk I mean milk that is brought from the country in the ordinary way into the city to be sold, not a drop of which is pure unless it is pasteurized or sterilized, -no medical man who has looked on the faces of these suffering children and felt his own inability to save their innocent lives, has been free from bitter heartache. Any medical man can picture to you the dying agonies of men and women in the prime of life who have left their families helpless, all for want of proper knowledge. Much has been said of tuberculosis and much has not yet been told. We can say the same things of typhoid fever, scarlet fever, and all the other unnecessary and

preventable diseases that are sweeping our people off the earth needlessly. It is simply because we have been used to these things, that our fathers and our forefathers have been used to them for generations, that we passively allow this dreadful waste of life. If laymen could see as clearly as medical men the needlessness of this loss and suffering, I do not believe we would wait a year or a month to take the first steps to remedy this terrible evil.
I do not wish to speak in detail of what a federal bureau of public health should do, but I take it for granted that its first step would be education-educate the people, teach them how they can avoid preventable disease, teach the cities how they must avoid disease, for .there is where the great slaughter comes. I have been told by some in authority that this is the work of the provinces. So it is the work of the provinces; it is the work of the cities, it is the work of the villages, it is the work of every individual. But I maintain that a federal bureau of public health would not interfere with the health departments of the provinces, but would rather be an educator to them, would be a stimulus and a guide to them. Such a bureau would teach the whole people more effectively than any provincial organization could do. But so far as my knowledge goes this question is as much a question for the federal authorities as for any of the provincial authorities. In the British North America Act, although among the fathers of confederation was one doctor-and he was a good doctor in his day as well as a pretty good politician-there is very little reference made to public health. I find only two clauses. The first section dealing with it defines the power of the federal government in this regard. They are to have charge of quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals. The Act assigns to the provinces:
The establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province other than marine hospitals.
In practice most of this work has been left to the provinces by the federal government, but I hope better days are coming and that the federal government will take hold of these things. There is much, Mr. Speaker, that a federal bureau of public health could do. As I said, its functions should be, for years to come, educative. Teach the people by literature, by public addresses, in every way possible, how to stop dying before their time. It is hardly worth while to go into details, there are so many of them I might mention. But the conditions in our factories all over the country, the unwholesome conditions in which men, women and little children work in our factories, are such as to require immediate 35
attention. The provinces, at least the province of Nova Scotia, have deemed it wise to appoint government inspectors of poor houses and prisons to see that sanitation regulations are carried out. Now, if a criminal's life is worth watching, how much more is the life of the bread earners worth watching, the men, women and children in our factories. Go into them to-day, go into them at any time until the summer heat and you will find many of them in the most unsanitary condition. Go into some of the Canadian mills, and you will find that the protection of the workers has never been considered. This is one of the very important things that a bureau of public health could look after. The school houses are unsanitary to a degree all over the country. They are a little better in the cities, but they are unsanitary to a degree in the country parts where I have known and seen them. We should provide for the examination of children in schools, the proper examination of our water supply, both in towns and country, for typhoid arises almost as frequently from the farm house well as from the river or lake supply of the city. Most people do not know this. I may say from experience in regard to the water supply in the towns of Nova Scotia, taking the stretch of country known as the Annapolis valley from the town of Windsor to the town of Annapolis, little less than 100 miles, in which there are from 12 to 15 towns and villages, that every doctor calculated on his autumn supply of typhoid fever arising from well water. In the last twenty years all those towns have been supplied with a magnificent water system from the mountains. On each side of the valley a pure supply of water comes into all those towns, and in those towns typhoid fever is unknown except that which is brought in by those who go to visit their country cousins, who have taken it from the farm house well. There is very little typhoid in the towns and villages except that which has been imported. Now, I say all these matters should be under the supervision of an official of the government, and the people should be instructed where to put their wells and how to keep them clean. I might go on and tell you what a board of health could do, but it would take me all night, and I would not be half done.
I said in the beginning, Mr. Speaker, that this question was a most important one. The medical profession have given the matter a great deal of earnest attention. If I did not fear to weary you I would like to run over what has been done by the medical associations of Canada and the appeals they have made to this good government of ours, for it is a good government. I would like to show what has been done by the Canadian Medical Asociation since 1902.



I do not know what was done before that, but I hold in my hand a record of what has been done since 1902. In 1902, at the thirty-fifth annual meeting of the Canadian Medical Association, the largest and most representative meeting of the medical profession up to that time, was held in the city of Montreal on the 16th, 17th and 18th of September. The following resolution was proposed by Dr. E. P. Lachapelle, Montreal, and seconded by Dr. J. R. Jones, of Winnipeg:
Resolved, that in the opinion of the Canadian Medical Association, now in session, the time is opportune for the Dominion government to earnestly consider the expediency of creating a separate department for public health, under one of the existing ministers, so that regulations, suggestions and correspondence, on such health matters as fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government, may be issued with the authority of a department of public health.
In 1903 a similar resolution was passed. I notice it is stated that the deputation that waited on the Prime Minister in 1903 was most courteously received. I am sure that could be said of the Prime Minister, not only in 1903, hut in every year since he has been in public life. They reported that he listened patiently to the sentiments set forth, and finally authorized Dr. Roddick to place a resolution on the order paper with a view to having a discussion in parliament before the Privy Council took up the matter in earnest. Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier also stated that in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, who was familiar with the whole question, he would not willingly go into the matter at a greater length with a view to legislation in the minister's absence. In 1904 there was another deputation, and a committee was appointed. In 1907 I had the pleasure myself of forming one of another deputation from the Canadian Medical Association that waited on Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Now, Mr. Speaker, I only mention these things to show that this is no new matter, the medical profession has been asking it for years. I feel sure that the reform will come, and that it will come soon. The finances of the country ask for it, the prosperity of the country requires it, suffering humanity demands it, dying men and women who have no need to die demand it. If we as a Christian people have caught the genius of Christianity, surely, in God's name, this reform will come and come soon, and I hope to see it before another year.

I wish to say a few words in support of the very important resolution which has been so ably and fully discussed this evening by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black). I must admit, however, that it appears he has left very little for me to say, and that little more should be required to be said.

He has treated the question so thoroughly, so correctly, and so exhaustively, that I think he surely must have miide an impression upon the government. It seems to me that the government, after hearing the facts he has stated, and after listening to the fund of information he has laid before the House, and the pointed, not to say alarming statements, he has made, should lose no time in taking action. He has clearly shown us that delay in a matter of this kind means to the Canadian people a loss not only of millions of dollars but also of thousands of lives. He has told us that 27,000 people die in Canada every year from preventable diseases, and he might very well have added that ten times, if, not fifty times, that number are compelled afterwards to go through life struggling, handicapped with weakened constitutions and to suffer the immense losses in time and in money which preventable sickness has entailed upon them. Preventive medicine has made such rapid progress during the last five or six years that perhaps those members of the government who are not medical men should be excused for not keeping themselves abreast of the times and not properly posting themselves in a matter of this kind. But, after to-day, they will scarcely be able to plead excusable ignorance in regard to this matter. If they would investigate and post themselves with regard to the works of the great masters in this line, of Prof. Koch, of Germany, and Pasteur, of France, they would very soon realize how very far behind the people of Canada are with regard to the question of preventive medicine. These great men, paid by their governments large salaries and furnished with well-equipped laboratories and assistants, have devoted their lives to this study and they have practically revolutionized the whole practice of medicine. They have pointed out to us not only how a great many diseases can be entirely prevented, especially those diseases that have their origin in germs, but they have also shown how, by a certain scientific line of treatment, people can be made immune to certain diseases. They have taught the medical profession that their first duty, as my hon. friend from Hants has said, is to keep the people well, is to keep them from getting sick, and they have shown them that there is truth in the old French adage that the best way to keep well is not to get sick. When we consider that nearly all the diseases which have their origin in germs can be prevented and that many others can be so managed that people would be immune to them, the government certainly have a very serious duty to perform in connection with the matter. We are spending $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 a year to prepare to meet an enemy that may never come to us; that is war or something of that kind.

It is nearly a hundred years since Canada was engaged in any foreign war and we are spending this large amount of money to meet an enemy that, if it did come here, would spare at least the poor children, women and old men. But there is an army invading our country at the present time that is taking away our people, that is slaughtering 27,000 every year and impoverishing a great many others. Are we going to make no effort to oppose this army? What we propose is that there should be a bureau of health established by the government, that it should be placed under the control of some well educated young Canadian, that he should have youth and a thorough education and that he should be competent to take the position as head of the department and conduct it in such a way as to ensure its success. He should be an enthusiast in his work and try to make for himself a name that would rival that of the great men of Europe. It should be his particular duty to study the particular diseases that are peculiar to this country and to instruct us in the best ways of avoiding them. It is scarcely fair that we should get all our information and all our benefit in this respect from France and Germany. These people are heavily taxed and still they put their hands in their pockets and pay these men to conduct these very necessary and useful experiments.
In the first place, the Dominion government have already certain departments of medicine established and all we would ask is that they be consolidated and that a proper head be placed over them. The Minister of Marine, as we have been told, looks after the marine hospitals; the Minister of the Interior looks after the inspection of immigrants; the Minister of Agriculture has his department of quarantine, and the Minister of Inland Revenue looks after the quality of our food; so that the Dominion government have already admitted that they have certain duties to perform in this matter. If these different departments were consolidated and the people were properly instructed, beneficial results would follow. They should be taught to use what God has given them; that is sunlight, and they should be shown what great advantage can be derived from the proper use of sunlight. If you go into many houses you will find that they are darkened, and if you ask the people why they will tell you that they do not wish to have flies in the house. The flies have more sense than the people; they will not stay in a darkened room. All these things could be pointed out, such as the advantage of pure, uncontaminated water and pure air. We know that there is a prejudice in the country against the open air. We know that although it is one of the principal things that are to be used in the cure of consumption, people who are trou-351
bled with lung disease have a special prejudice against the open window. This should be all explained to them, and the injury resulting from the use of contaminated air should also be pointed out. The government have already taken the responsibility of sending out a very useful pamphlet with regard to the spread of tuberculosis. It was prepared by our good friend, Mr. H. H. Miller, M.P., and the government took the responsibility of having it printed and of having a large number of copies circulated through the country. This action of the government is calculated to do a great deal of good. Why have they not sent out other pamphlets on these lines? Why have they not sent a pamphlet telling the people that it is absolutely unnecessary that people should have typhoid fever? Look at the number who are dying all over the country as the result of typhoid fever. This disease as the hon. member for Hants explaind, is entirely unnecessary. If the dejecta from every typhoid fever patient were at once cremated or disinfected in a proper manner we would very soon have no typhoid fever in the Dominion of Canada. Similarly in the case of smallpox. I remember very well, in 1848 and 1849, when the famine was in Ireland and Scotland, that there was an immense immigration into this country, and I remember, although I was only a small boy, that I noticed that the older people who came from the old country were covered with pock-marks. It was supposed that every person should have smallpox at some time in his life; yet, see how few people have it now. It is not more than 200 years since a slave was advertised to be sold in Montreal and one of the principal recommendations in regard to that slave was that he had had the smallpox. We know that there is a feeling abroad in the country that every child must have scarlet fever, whooping cough and measles at some time. Yet, it is not necessary that children should have any of these diseases. These diseases are all absolutely preventable. There is another class of disease which is just as easily preventable, and the people should be instructed in regard to them. I refer to the diseases resulting from improper dieting and the improper use and mastication of food. People should be taught that food is the fuel consumed in the human system and that therefore it should be carefully regulated according to the amount and quality of the work to be done. They should be carefully instructed and told that men who are engaged in heavy, active, out-door manual labour require much more food than those who are engaged in inside sedentary employments.	.	,
You may go along any back line in the country and you may come to some wayside cheese factory or saw-mill and if you ask the old engineer there he will tell you that

if he continued to add fuel to the frre after the machinery had ceased to work he would very soon ruin the engine or burst the boiler. People seldom exercise so much good judgment in regard to their own systems. The wealthy and those who have least to do often take the most food and of the richest and strongest kind. They can afford it; it looks aristocratic and it pleases their taste and their appetite, but medical men can tell them that very often the consequences are disease and death. When more food is taken into the system than can be assimilated or is necessary for the nourishment of the body, the surplus simply goes to decay and turns to poison in the stomach and intestines. Nature makes an effort to get rid of these poisonous materials through the bowels, the liver, the kidneys, the skin and other excretory organs; but if this over indulgence is continued for many years as it often is these excretory organs become exhausted; they gradually fail to do their duty, the blood and the system become loaded up, with effete, and worn out, and poisonous material and the foundation is laid for many dangerous and fatal diseases. Therefore the people should be instructed as to the quality and quantity of the food they should take. More, they should be carefully instructed also that the food should be properly cooked and how to cook it. They should be told also that in every case food should be carefully and very thoroughly masticated and mixed with the saliva. In fact, in every case the food should be retained in the mouth until it is not only chewed into a pulp but until it is perfectly mixed with the saliva which is a highly important digestive ingredient. You often hear people say their teeth water when we know as a matter of fact that no water comes from the teeth, but we do know there is thrown out a fluid from the . salivary glands of the mouth to assist in the very important act of digestion which is carried on in the mouth, a fact which is very often forgotten by people when they are taking their food. It should be represented to the people that even the softest of food such as porridge and mashed potatoes should be carefully and thoroughly mixed with the saliva before it is swallowed, and that the food should be moistened with the saliva which nature intended to moisten it. Tea and coffee, and even milk, and water, or any of these fluids have no digestive power, and if we insist in bolting our food in large chunks and washing it down with these or any other fluids we need not wonder if we are troubled with indigestion. The saliva is an alkiline fluid and it is necessary that it should chemically combine with the acid gastric juice of the stomach to set up and continue the proper and healthy process of digestion, and therefore the food should be prepared in the mouth before passing to the system. morsel of food should be taken into the mouth and thoroughly mixed with the saliva and then well masticated before it is swallowed. The right quantity of fluid should be taken of course, but it should be taken at the right time. In the country, especially in the winter, I have found as a medical man that there is a great mistake made in regard to the amount of fluid that should be taken. There are two mistakes made by the people who are not engaged in heavy labour in the winter and this applies even to farmers; they take more food than they require and a great deal less fluid than is necessary. In taking this fluid it should be taken in a proper way. They may drink between meals or between bites if they choose, but a person who is troubled with dyspepsia or weakened stomach trouble should never take fluid into his mouth while food is there. Then again, starchy foods and meats should be particularly well chewed. If they are not, they simply rot and go to decay in the inside, and what more dangerous material could you have internally than rotten meat or fermenting and decaying vegetables? And if we persist deliberately in thus making graveyards of our stomachs is it any wonder that we find our own way to the cemetery? Then again I would neither advise nor recommend that we should give the children in the schools and the people throughout the country a course in anatomy, nor yet that we should give them much more than a mere indication, as I have given you, of the information that may be given to them in regard to digestion. But we can teach and publish pamphlets that will convey to them some idea about the functions and the care of the human system. There is no more important study in which men can engage than an investigation of the proper and healthy workings of their own bodies. I think there are few people who will deny that. Is it not strange then that we can find many who thoroughly understand the most intricate workings of other machinery but who at the same time appear to know or care little about their own systems; about the necessity for a rigid and faithful observance of the simple laws that govern the healthy action of their own bodies. Farmers and mechanics and others appear to know well that by taking proper care of their agricultural implements and other instruments of labour, these can be made not only to work better but to last longer. Every engineer knows distinctly that he must thoroughly understand a locomotive before he is allowed to take charge of one on a railroad. Even the boy with a bicycle is well aware that it must be regularly oiled and cleaned and cared for or its usefulness will soon be gone and ultimately it will be ruined. Let us take another example-that of the fashionable and fastidious young man who drives his own touring car
