through the country and who becomes so enamoured of and interested in its workings that he forgets all about his costly clothing and so utterly disregards appearances that you will see him lying prone on the road, on his back, gazing upwards to see what has gone wrong with the machinery of his automobile. In all probability he regards that machine simply as a toy to be laid aside without profit at the close of a summer holiday, and yet, foolishly we think, he gives it his very best attention and his very best care, while one-half the earnest attention given to the study of the structure and workings of his own body might add many years to his life and save him from an immense amount of disease and suffering. The human machine is an automobile far more valuable and important than the most elaborate touring car that ever was conceived and perfected. Yet, notwithstanding all this every human being, every man and woman in the country, is compelled to take charge of and run a machine, their own bodies, that is far more complicated and interesting and far more difficult to manage than any of these I have mentioned. Few fit themselves properly for the task, and the result is, what the member for Hants indicated this evening, that after spending a whole lifetime in the practice of medicine I state here that in my opinion most of the sickness and far more than one-half the deaths which occur in this country before sixty years of age are due either directly or indirectly to ignorance of the laws of health and of nature or to carelessness in applying them. Now, this study could be made interesting to the public. The people could be instructed in regard to the functions of their own bodies; they could be shown that the human machine is a wonderful piece of mechanism and the wonderful working of it could be pointed out to them in an attractive new way. It could be demonstrated to them that by having even a partial knowledge of the peculiar functions of the human body they might extend their lives for many many years. I happened to notice in a paper yesterday that some insurance company is proposing to send out literature to those it insured, and it makes the statement definitely that the period of human life could be extended by fifteen years.
As I have said, the human machine is a wonderful piece of mechanism. Its beauty, symmetry, elasticity, strength and adaptability are so perfect that the result is simply amazing. If a man constructs a great number of machines for a certain purpose, they are usually so much alike that one cannot be distinguished from another. But that is not the case with nature's great Master Mechanic. There are said to be over four hundred millions of people on the earth's surface. Each one of these has an organism of his own; and yet no two of them are exactly alike. Notwithstanding this wonderful variation, the structure of the human system is so perfect that if it were run in every case in accordance with the dictates of common sense and the law of nature, I believe that it would, barring accidents, last about a hundred years. But in many cases not only are the dictates of common sense ignored, but the laws of health and of nature are so neglected and violated that the result is simply appalling.
The study of the human system might do our people good in more ways than one, because I cannot understand how any man who becomes familiar with its structure and operation can believe that it took its present form by chance or accident or even by gradual development. There are so many evidences of design in it that there must have been a designer, and that the designer must have been able to create. For my part, I cannot comprehend how any man can thoroughly apprehend the wonders of his own body, and be an unbeliever or an atheist. For, after all, the greatest mechanical achievements effected by mankind have been simply poor imitations of nature and of nature's great Designer, Creator and Controller. For example, the telegraph is supposed to be a recent invention but it has been long in use in tEe human system. The brain is, as it were, a central electric station, from which the mind, with wonderful accuracy and rapidity, sends forth its messages to every part of the body. Think of a lady at a piano, think of the rapidity of her fingers and the accuracy of the sounds produced, and reflect that her performance is governed by a little electric cell located in the brain. Some doctor has said that the human brain occupies less space in proportion to its capabilities than any other machine ever invented. It sends forth a nerve to every ultimate fibre of some five hundred muscles, to every pin-head area of the various glands which keep the machine oiled and heated and cooled. On the surface of the average human body there are sixteen square feet of skin, which is so completely covered with nervous fibre, that the point of a pin eanot find a spot unguarded. Similarly our ears are nature's perfect telephone, and Bell's is only an imitation. The telephonic switchboard of the brain is remarkable for its accuracy and completeness. Then, again, the telescope is only an enlarged representation of the eye of man or an animal. Just stop for one minute and consider if some little chance or accident had entered into the location of the eye. Consider how its delicate mechanism is guarded by the brows, the lids, the lashes and the solid bony structure around it. Think how inconvenient it would have been if our eyes had happened to be located in the soles of the feet. How liable the delicate

structures would have been to injury or destruction ; and think how humiliating and annoying it would have been to our young men if they had been compelled to sit down and take off their shoes and stockings and hold up their feet every time they wanted to look at a beautiful young woman or some other interesting - object. Then, suppose, our mouths had happened to be located in the backs of our necks. Food would have reached the gullet just as well, but it would have been very inconvenient to have been compelled to carry the porridge and milk and the toast and tea of our breakfast around to that part of our body in the morning. The old saying that there is many a slip between the cup and the lip would in that case have been still more appropriate. Then, consider how inconvenient it would have been if our ears had been located on our elbows or under our arms. I might go on with illustrations of this kind to show that the human body is not the result of chance or accident. There are evidences of design in every part of it. Every organ not only adds to the beauty and symmetry of the system, but is so located as to be in the best possible position to do its duty easily and effectively. Think, for example, of the way in which the human system is guarded in the matter of food. First, we have two sharp sentrie_s, the eyes, so located that they can see everything that enters the mouth. The food has to pass their scrutiny first. Then, as it enters the mouth, its savoury or unsavoury condition is challenged by two other sentries, the nostrils. Next the lips test its hardness or softness. Then it is met by thirty-two sturdy sentries, all clad in white and drawn up in battle array; these are the teeth, which subject the food .to careful examination lest some foreign or deleterious substance may be covered up in it and thus smuggled into the system. While they are doing their duty, there stands behind them another sentinel, the sense of taste. But it is quite possible that the food, having passed these guards and undergone these examinations, might still contain some little invisible germs that succeeded in passing through after all. These are searched out by the saliva, which is thrown out by six other sentinels three on either side of the mouth. It is well to remember that the saliva is poisonous to these germs, that if it is well mixed with the food, it will destroy even typhoid germs, but when the food is taken rapidly into the stomach, the saliva does not have a chance to do its full work. Then, if something deleterious should succeed in getting past all these guards or sentinels, the very moment it reaches the stomach, a telegraphic message is sent from the brain ordering that the dangerous intruder shall be ejected. I or any other medical man in the House Mr. THOS. CHISHOLM.
could go on and give examples to show how this kind of literature could be made interesting to the public and do a great deal of good. It should be made readable, and it should be free from Greek or Latin phrases and from technical terms. It should be given in simple language and in a common sense way; and if the people were instructed in this way, I am satisfied that they would be greatly benefited. This is the kind of work that should be taken up by ai bureau of health. I could go on all night describing the beauties of the respiratory system, the circulatory system or the secretory system.
In every branch of the subject we find equal wonders and equal perfections. This would be the work of a Bureau of Health and I do hope the government will turn their attention to this matter and adopt an intelligent and aggressive policy. They can at least prevent ignorance, and it is ignorance that is causing the death of so many of our little children and of our grown up people. Much has been done in the prevention of tuberculosis, but it is a pity that this work has been left too largely to private subscriptions and private enterprise. I am sure that when the government consider and fully understand this matter, they will bring honour to themselves and great benefit to the country by instituting a federal bureau of health. As to the argument that the provinces will take it up, there is work for the provinces, work for the cities, work for the county councils, for the township councils, and for the school sections. There is no place where more can be done than right in the school, as I have said. The schools should be inspected, the children should be instructed, and diseases should be checked in the school room in their inception. I am convinced that if we expect to become the great people we should on this continent, the dominating people as I am sure we ultimately will, we mu$t be a healthy people. All we can ask the government to do is to vote just one half the amount of money spent each year in unnecessary funerals in Canada; if they will do that we will have a bureau of health that will astonish the world. If they will vote for this purpose one-fourth of what they spend in bringing immigrants to Canada, we will fill the places of these immigrants with healthy Canadians. I would ask that they would take some action in this matter without further delay. I have great pleasure in seconding the motion so ably moved by my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black). I am sure he did it in all unselfishness, and I would be glad if he and I, in our old days in the profession, could be the pioneers in securing this great good for the country before we. leave our places in the House and in the profession. I hope the young medical men, the

clergymen, the newspapers and every man in this House will preach this new gospel of sanitation and press on until we have in Canada a thoroughly healthy and prosperous people.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. H. McALISTER (King's and Albert).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great pleasure to the addresses of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. T. Chisholm) who have so ably proposed this resolution. But, Sir, I was surprised indeed to notice how little attention was paid to the subject by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House. It is one of the most important questions that have been discussed in the House this year or that will be,, yet gentlemen left the chamber, one half of those who remained went to sleep, and one quarter did not pay attention. If I cared to do so I could make half the, members now here leave the chamber and could empty the galleries by saying there are millions of microbes in this chamber. Suppose there is a consumptive in the gallery to-night, as I have quite strong reason to believe there is, and if that lady should expectorate once on the floor, how many germs do you suppose would be put into circulation? One million.
The object of the resolution we are discussing is to enlighten our people along these lines, to prevent the people with that disease coming to a place like this, and to teach them how to take care of their sputum and to sterilize that which would cause infection. It may be said that this is not a matter for this government. Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of tremendous importance. I am sorry to say there are too many people in Canada who are not aware of the dangerous germs that are in existence. Pathologists have proved beyond a doubt that all diseases are transmitted by germs. When I had typhoid fever some 19 years ago, it was not known that that disease was caused- by a germ, but since then it has been proven beyond a doubt that it is a germ disease. What are these little germs like? Like the little pollywogs in the water. It would be interesting, if time would permit, to describe the development of these germs in the water, their entrance and the great battle which takes place between this germ, the typhoid baccillus, and the lencocyte in the blood. This conflict generates a poison called a potomaine, which in many instances creates sufficient constitutional disturbances to cause death. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) told you of the number of deaths from typhoid fever, and I have no reason to doubt the correctness of his figures. He could have told you there are thousands and thousands dying of tuberculosis today, from a disease caused by germs, and that the death of these people was un-Mr. McALISTER.
necessary, that the disease could be banished from our country if certain precautions were taken. That is what the government should realize, they should become seized of the idea that this thing can be done, and as my hon. friend says the time has come when it must be done. As an illustration of the manner in which typhoid can be checked, in our little town of Sussex, I myself had as many as eleven cases of typhoid at one time before the installation of a waterworks system. I was myself almost ignorant how these people were being infected by the bacilli, and I am safe in saying that not three per cent of the inhabitants realized what was causing the disease. They were using water from wells which were contaminated from cess pools, &c. Every year we lost from three to six people from that little town. Some six years ago the waterworks were installed, the water was taken from a river that was perfectly pure and was run into a filter. Since then there has not been a case of typhoid in the town. That shows that typhoid fever can be done away with if the proper precautions are taken and it is the duty of the government, I believe, to prevent the pollution of our rivers. Take Montreal, for instance, where they have a great epidemic of typhoid. I believe the federal government should take that up and force the city of Montreal to instal a filtration system. My hon. friend beside me (Mr. M. Martin) who is an alderman of the city of Montreal, tells me they are going to spend $2,000,000 this year in trying to escape from that dreaded disease typhoid. I presume they will seek to do this by installing a filtration plant.
It does not matter about the cost; it is not a matter of money at all, it is too serious a proposition for that. We are very careful, as has been nobly said by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black), that the dumb animals should be protected and half a million dollars a year is expended to protect them. Why, then, should not human beings be protected? They ought to be. I confess that I myself am afraid of the bacillus tuberculosis. I feel that I have in my constitution appropriate soil for its growth. Some claim that tuberculosis is not hereditary. I know it is hereditary, in this sense, that, while a child may not be born with consumption, it may be born with a delicate mucous membrane of the air passage, inherited from father or mother, associated with a weak resistance, so that when the germ comes it grows like an oat in soil that has been prepared for its reception. Medical men know that patients come to them sometimes and say that they have a cough, have not felt well, associated with emaciation and night sweats. These symptoms date from a cold. The cold did not give them consumption; it

only prepared the mucous membrane of the air passage, so that when the germ was taken in it took root and grew and formed a nucleus for the dreaded disease. We spend thousands of dollars a year in bringing foreigners into this country to become citizens and live under the dear old flag. It is estimated, as the hon. member for Hants has shown, that the average male inhabitant, able to keep himself and others, is worth $1,000 to the country under whose flag he lives. We must bring in immigrants because we are not prolific enough to populate this country otherwise. If we are bringing in others, why not protect those we already have? Thousands of our people are dying every year who could be saved from dying; we want this government to show the people how to live. I am not looking for a job myself, and I do not want to go around the country lecturing, but I do not see how a better thing could be done by this government than to employ one or both of the hon. members who moved and seconded this resolution to speak to public audiences, to instruct the people in the germ theory, teach them how to be careful of their health, explain to them, if they have a consumptive in their house, how to destroy the sputum, and so on. It is wonderful what can be accomplished in this way if we take the necessary means to do it. We do not expect the government to do everything-and it would be a bad thing for us young doctors if they did. I am not surprised to hear these statements from the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Thos. Chisholm), for it seems to me they will not be practising medicine very much longer-I think they expect to remain in politics for the rest of their lives; they must be looking for a senatorship, or they would not talk as they do. If the government will do what these gentlemen ask it to do they wall accomplish one of the greatest reforms ever accomplished in Canada. The hon. member for East Huron made a remark on which I would like to enlarge. He said that we eat too much. There is no doubt about it. More people in the Dominion of Canada and the United States, and all over the world, die of overeating than of overdrinking.
Oh, oh.

That may seem a bold statement to make, but I mean it and I am ready to stand by it. The hon. member for East Huron explained that when people take too much into their stomach it lies there and causes poisoning. But I propose to go further than that. If the stomach is in good condition it will digest far more than the system requires. The little glands or ducts take up more than is necessary and thus it is carried into the circulation. The Mr. McALISTER.
human system is a machine and requires only so much to keep it going. If more than is needed is forced into the circulation it causes dilatation of the circulatory system which is made up of capillaries, veins and arteries. These are muscles like any other. If you exercise the muscles of your arms for half an hour a day, development will take place. If too much of the products from food is forced into the capillaries, veins and arteries, the arteries are going to become enlarged. They do not become stronger as the muscles of your arms become stronger with exercise, but they become weaker, and that makes an old man out of a young one. A man is as old as his arteries, not his years.
However, that is a little aside from the subject and is more than I intended to say. In fact, I am not prepared to say very much on this subject and I will not trouble the House for more than a few moments longer. In conclusion, I would say that this subject should receive the earnest and sincere consideration of every member of this House. I am not saying that because I am a medical man. But I am a firm believer in the germ theory. I was taught that in old McGill, by Professor Adami, who is an excellent authority on pathology, and I have proven it for myself in my own practice that practically every disease is associated with some germ. Of these there are three we should particularly ward against, the tubercular bacillus, the typhoid bacillus and the diphtheria bacillus. And in that fight we should have the assistance of the federal government. Just how this is to be done, of course, is a matter to be worked out by the government itself. I hope that both sides of the House will see their way clear to support this resolution. And, in that connection, let me call attention to the fact that these germs attack Liberals and Conservatives alike.

It is not my intention to take up much time discussing this resolution, so ably proposed by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black)! and so exhaustively dealt with by the hon. member for East Huron (Mr. T. Chisholm) and the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. McAllister). The resolution calls upon the government of Canada to perfect an organization whereby present scientific knowledge would be made practically available for the suppression of preventable diseases. I observed that the hon. gentleman who preceded me dwelt upon scientific methods to be used in preventing disease. I think that probably enough time has been taken up in impressing the members of this House of the wonders of the human body, and of the desirability of preventing disease so far as we possibly can.

Certainly I think this question is one deserving the most careful consideration on the part of every member of this House. Let me mention particularly one argument made use of by the hon. gentleman who so ably proposed this resolution, I mean the figures he gave showing the number of deaths which occur annually in Canada from preventable diseases. Mr. Speaker, those figures reveal a serious condition of affairs, and I would ask this House to consider them carefully.
I think that was the strongest point in the argument made by the hon. member for Hants. If, not 27,000, not 20,000, not 5,000, but if only 1,000, persons in the Dominion of Canada die annually whose deaths could be prevented by any Act of this legislature, certainly you will agree that it is the duty of this legislature to try to prevent that loss of life. We are well acquainted with the old adage that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. I think we all subscribe to that statement. While medical science has done a great deal in the past to lengthen the span of life, and we have been furnished by certain departments of this government with the facts proving that in the last 25 years the average length of human life has been increased, the facts that have been brought to our attention tonight must have convinced us that still more can be done in the same direction. If it is a good thing to cure disease, it is a far better thing to prevent it. I feel convinced that before the end of this century men will occupy the seats we are filling today who will look back to the early years of this present century and wonder that the parliament of Canada was so apathetic over a matter of such great national importance.

I agree with much that has been said by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House as to the importance of the question which has been brought to our attention by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black). We have been told how much medical science has done in late years to prolong human life, but it is sad to reflect that medical men themselves have not been the greatest beneficiaries of the increased discoveries in medical science. The farmers of our country, and the members of the learned professions other than the medical profession, have benefited from the advances made by medical science more than the members of the medical profession themselves. Now when we come to consider the resolution calling upon this government to take action, we are led to inquire whether the fathers of confederation were wise in relegating to the different provinces the subject of public health, giving them charge of that most important question. We are led to ask ourselves whether the Dominion government are better constituted to deal
with that question than are the provincial governments. While I do not wish to differ from hon. gentlemen who have .preceded me,
I am still doubtful whether we could do more towards accomplishing the object we all have in view by asking the Dominion government to deal with this matter than by leaving it to the provinces. For my part I am of the opinion that the provincial governments can work out this problem better than the Dominion government. We know that in several provinces the local governments have made great strides in the past few years in the direction of improving public health. Take for instance the province of Ontario, with which I am best acquainted. We all know what great strides that province has been making iin that direction the last few years. In every municipality they have a health officer; the municipal council appoints a health officer, and generally chooses him from amongst the best medical men they have. It is the duty of this officer to visit every person that is infected with disease, to examine into the environment, into the water supply, which we all know is one of the greatest sources of disease. It is his duty to look into the milk supply, and to ascertain if possible the cause of every outbreak of contagious disease. Now do you think that a Dominion health bureau could accomplish more than is being done by the provincial health bureau? Is it not possible that there might be an overlapping of duties, that there might be friction between the two bodies? What more can be done than is being done at the present time? We are making rapid strides along that line already. We know that every house has to be placarded in which there is infectious disease. If the average length of human life has been prolonged twenty or twenty-five years, I believe it is due to the provincial machinery, to the work that is accomplished by the health officers in the different provinces. Therefore, before we ask the federal government to appoint a federal health bureau, we should consider this question very carefully. Of course I would not suggest for a moment that any medical man wanted a federal bureau appointed for the purpose of getting an office. So far as medical men are concerned, I believe they are far above any monetary consideration whatever. But this is a question which we should consider before any more steps are taken along that line. It is possible for us to make that machinery more perfect and it is wise for us to do so. That machinery is being made more perfect each year. As far as Toronto is concerned, we have probably, at the head of tha bureau, a number of the best medical men in Canada, and I believe they are accomplishing great work, a work that could not be accomplished by other bureaus in Can-
COMMONS*
ada. Any outbreak is immediately reported to them and if necessary they send experts. We have not only that, but we have, in connection with our agricultural societies a woman's institute. They come around and deliver practical lectures in connection with cooking. They bring with them material and in the presence of our wives and daughters demonstrate the advantage of cooking in relation to the health of the community. They show how food can be more easily digested and they tell the people the kind of food that can best be taken in. That movement is both useful and practical. I can come to no other conclusion than that the fathers of confederation were wise in their day in leaving to the provincial authorities to work out this problem. I believe that much has been accomplished and that much can yet be accomplished for the good of mankind. We may say that every life we can save is a matter of great importance, but there is another side to this question. We might ask ourselves the question, what the Dominion government has done since confederation as compared with the work of the provincial boards of health, and I submit that the achievements will not stand comparison, that the provincial government have done much more along this line and that the Dominion government, in so far as they are working out the problem, have not accomplished what they should have.
Does the hon. gentleman take into consideration that there are other provinces outside of Ontario making up this Dominion?

I might tell the hon. gentleman something that he probably does not know and that is that there is not a province in the Dominion of Canada that I have not visited, and that there is not a provincial board of health whose work I have not looked into. I must say that while some are not up to the province of Ontario with respect to the promotion of public health, they are doing an important work. But, if my hon. friend's province is not up to the standard he should turn his attention to that and bring it up to such a standard that it will be capable of dealing with this important question. I think they are dealing in a fairly effective manner with this question in all of the provinces, but I think Ontario is the banner province in this respect. Our hospitals are year by year becoming better equipped^ and the officers of these institutions are doing their work well. The trained nurses throughout the country have accomplished probably as much as the medical profession have. These two, the trained nurses and the medical profession, working hand in hand, have accomplished a great deal of good. Now, we might ask ourselves the question if the marine hospitals under the Mr. BARR.
control of the Dominion government are better than are the hospitals in the cities and towns of the different provinces. I have visited one or two marine hospitals and I have been unable to find any superiority in them although the work they are doing is very good.
Now, let us turn our attention to the question of the medican inspection of immigrants coming in to this country. I have travelled in other lands, I have visited the older countries, I have watched the course pursued by the medical men with respect to our immigration, and I must say that theii methods are perfectly outrageous. I was surprised not long ago at what I saw at one of our ports. A boat came in with a large number of immigrants. The health officers stood there and passed those immigrants at the rate of from seven to eleven a minute. I took the time. There were immigrants passed that were a curse to this country. I saw these officers passing men who were not healthy. We have had immigrants admitted to this country affected by a certain disease of the eye, they have brought that disease into Canada anil it has not been stamped out. Yet, the medical health officers looked on while these people passed. Their instructions were that they must not impede the landing of the immi grants. They had only a given time and the result was that men, women and child ren passed these officers who ought not to have been allowed to come into this country and would not have been allowed to enter the United States if they had attempted to go there. Is it possible that medical men can examine two or three hundred immigrants at the rate they were passing off the boat which was under my observation. There were those that were not healthy in many respects, men, women and children afflicted with diseases that had been handed down to them from them fathers and grandfathers and yet they were allowed to become citizens of this country. Go to our hospitals and compare the number of immigrants that are in these institutions with the number of patients drawn from our own population and you find there are ten immigrants to one native born, proving beyond a doubt that a large amount of the disease that we have in this country is traceable to immigrants who are coming in from Europe and even from England, Ireland and Scotland. If this parliament would inaugurate a good system of inspection it would be a good thing for the country. First, before the immigrants ,enter the boat they should be submitted to a careful examination by competent medical men and then, when they land in this country, they should be carefully gone over once more and every man, woman and child, should be turned back who is not* healthy. If we adopted this system wei would accomplish more for the he rlth of the country than we could hope to accom-

plish by the creation of such a bureau as has been proposed, which would probably clash with the health departments of the different provinces and accomplish very little good If the government and the medical men of this country would turn attention to that question, they would accomplish more than they could by the formation of a bureau of health as far as th$ Dominion is concerned. Under these circumstances, I think the first thing to be done will be to take this question into consideration and until it is demonstrated that we can accomplish more than the pro-i vincial boards of health have done we had better leave the question to be dealt with by them.

Mr. Speaker, since I took a seat in this House thirty-one years ago this important question has from time to time engaged its attention. We have discussed it over and over again and yet it seems to me that in all that time we have made but very little headway. It has been claimed by some that we have made a good deal of headway lately. While we have done some things that are commendable we have left undone, in my judgment, many things which we might very well have done. The hon. member who moved this motion (Mr. Black) spoke of the number of people who die annually that might be saved, the number being stated at over 20,000. Every member of the House, whether he be a medical man or not, will agree that it is desirable to reduce the death rate, and we agree also that it is in our power to reduce the death rate from preventable diseases. The professional science of the age has given us the means to prevent consumption, typhoid fever, diphtheria, scarlet fever, smallpox, and other such diseases if we only use the right means. On the possibility of stamping out these diseases, the medical profession is unanimous and I think it will be admitted they are competent judges on that point. One hon. member instanced that if a lady in the gallery who might be infected with tuberculosis should expectorate down on the floor of this House millions of bacilli would be liberated, causing danger to every member in this chamber. That illustration brought home the danger to us in a very forcible way, but I wondered at the time if he thought of the 'germane' that was on that side of the House all the time and to what danger gentlemen over there were exposed, not to say anything about those on this side. One of the gentlemen on the other side told us that the great thing was to educate, educate, that if we put our present day knowledge into practice we would attain the end we desire. But, as I understand we are met right here in this parliament with an insurmountable difficulty and that is that our constitution does not give the federal government the power to establish a bureau of health, I remember that about thirty years ago a very important deputation waited upon the government of that day and represented the importance of establishing a bureau of health. Those who take the trouble to read the debates of the period will see that the ground was intellir gently covered by many eminent medical men who were then members of this House. The government desired to do something in the direction of mitigating the evils pointed out by the deputation, but, Sir Charles Tup-per, and Sir John Macdonald and I think the' Minister of Justice drew attention to the fact that while we could deal with quarantine and marine hospitals, anything further in that direction would be infringing on the rights of the provinces. That deputation pressed on the government the wisdom of amending the British North America Act so as to give the federal government the power, and it seems to me that until we do amend the British North America Act we cannot do any very effective work. In my judgment it would be an easy thing to amend the British North America Act if we brought together representatives of the different provinces, and ol tne boards of health throughout the Dominion, and of the medical association, and agreed to present a petition to the Imperial parliament to amend the constitution. I think, Sir Charles Tupper did make representations to this end to the home secretarv of that date, but he left political life m Canada at that time and we were deprived ol his valuable services and everything seemed to drop just then. But what was done was not all lost. There was a sum of money voted by the federal parliament for the purpose of supporting a health journal which was pu -lished for a great many years and which had an important, educative effect. We went further and provided for the collection of mortuary statistics and endeavoured to so tabulate them that the percentage of deaths from the various diseases could be ascertained. But what has always been the mystery of my life is that while we think it is justifiable to spend millions of dollars a year bringing immigrants to our shores we deem it necesary to vote only $500,000 for the purpose of endeavouring to reduce the death rate amongst our own people who are our most valuable citizens. There is where I think we have been short-sighted and parsimonious. I notice Sir, that while former motions of this nature called for the establishment of a board of health, this motion simply states that the time has arrived when the government of Canada shall perfect organization whereby present scientific knowledge would be made practically available for the prevention of preventable
diseases.	, ,,
If that is all we ask the government, they have no excuse. They cannot say that it is

not in our power to do that. There is no obstruction from the standpoint of the British North America Act; there is no interference with the rights of the provinces. We can do that by voting money enough to educate the people, to distribute this knowledge, to publish all the pamphlets and fly sheets we like. But I think we should go further than that. I think we should have a department or bureau of health, and we could very well have it without in any way coming in conflict with the important work that is being done by the various provinces. What is more, I think we should have some such conference as was suggested a few years ago, that would enable us to pass a law that would bring every medical association and teaching body in Canada under one medical clause, which would give a medical man power to cross the boundary line from Quebec to Ontario or from Ontario to Que-bee or from Ontario to Manitoba, wherever it was necessary to save life and promote public health. I regret that when that attempt was made, many members of this House prevented it being accomplished. Does it not show a narrow-mindedness and selfishness on our part that we are not desirous of doing all the good we can in this respect? If medical men have not the liberality to do this, we simply show the world that our profession has not attained that importance that it ought to have attained long ago. But leaving that aside, what can the federal government do? It can do all that this resolution asks. It can grant the money to edueate._ It can use its own machinery for issuing and distributing the pamphlets, papers, fly sheets, and everything else necessary to educate, without infringing on the rights of any province or any portion of the country. It is said that great forces move slowly, i Well, parliament must be a great force, for it certainly moves very slowly in regard to this subject.
I	have not taken the interest in it of late years that I did in my early life in this House, because it seems to be almost a waste of time to discuss it here, so little attention is given to it. I have noticed that when it is discussed, most of the members leave the House. At the present time there are only about 10 on the other side ?{ *use fnd. a few more on this side.
II	that is an indication of all the interest that parliamentarians in this country take in this important Question, I do not wonder that parliament moves slowly. If we were unanimous in our desire and .aim and stood by each other in our effort to obtain it, there is no government in the world that could refuse us, especially if we asked only what is asked in this resolution. Even if we went further, and asked the government to try to get an amendment made to the British North America Act conferring on the federal parliament the right and authority to deal with this subject, we could get that without very much trouble. We do not seem to be as

sincere and energetic and unanimous as we profess to be, or we would accomplish very much more than we do. I can only say that I agree with everything that has been said on this subject to-night, and it has been a mystery to me why we have not made greater progress than we have. The government have done something, but they could do a great deal more, and I hope the day will soon come when they will take up this important subject and do something not only for the benefit of the present generation but for the benefit of posterity as well.

I wish to congratulate the mover of this motion not only on the spirit which prompted him to bring the question to the attention of the House at this early stage of the session, but also on the large-heartedness which has induced him to study the question and show such a complete mastery of it as he has done to-night. We might reasonably expect this from a doctor in a large practice, who has given so much of his life to the care of humanity. It is essentially a question which the medical fraternity can discuss in its details and in its professional aspect much better than those of us who are only laymen. But still it is a question which affects and interests every one in the Dominion, whether lay or professional. It comes very closely home to the family life of the country, and there is no doubt in Canada to-day a vast mass of ignorance in regard to the commonest precautions against disease, the dispelling of which is very important to the economic progress and welfare of our country. As my hon. friend who has just sat down says, this is an old question in the House of Commons. It is a complicated question, because it interferes to a certain extent with the constitutional rights of the provinces. We have discussed these time and time again. I will not go into any details with regard to them to-night, because most of us are familiar with them. I will only point out that several of the questions brought up tonight and put forward as arguments in favour of a motion of this kind are so evidently connected with that portion of the public health which is directly relegated to the provincial legislatures, that we cannot touch upon them all. One gentleman spoke of sanitation and drainage. My hon. friend who moved the resolution spoke of the way in which typhoid fever is disseminated by wells. This is a question which is entirely local in its character, entirely within the purview of the municipal and provincial authorities as a question of public health. It does not come within our purview in any way whatever, and nothing we could do in a legislative or legal way could touch it. One hon. gentleman, I think the hon. mem-

ber for Dufferin (Mr. Barr), spoke of the health officers all through the country, in the province of Ontario especially. That is true, and it is also true of other provinces, I suppose of all the provinces. I can say myself, from knowledge of the province of Quebec, that in all the municipalities and parishes of our province there are health officers whose duty it is to look after the public health and to carry out the sanitary regulations provided for under the provincial laws. My hon. friend who has just spoken expressed his desire to have the whole medical profession and practice assimilated, so that a medical man in one province, having obtained his degree in medicine, should be entitled to practise in all parts of the country. My hon. friend will remember that not many years ago this House discussed that question, and an Act was put upon the statute-book entitled, I think, 'The Medical Council Act.' So jealous were the members of the medical profession themselves of their rights in each province and so fearful was this parliament of overstepping the bounds of provincial rights and prerogatives, that we were obliged to say that the Act would only apply and come into force in anv province when the province itself had adopted it.
It could only come into force when all the provinces had adopted it.

Still worse. And up to the present time, although it is six or seven years since the Act was passed, it has not come into force, evidencing that this is a question which is hedged about by very difficult problems. It is one which we cannot deal with lightly and if we deal with it in, any way that I can conceive of, we would run the risk of very soon treading upon the privileges and prerogatives of the medical profession or those jealous of provincial rights; and the likelihood is we would be stopped in a great deal of our work.
I confess myself to have so much sympathy with the motives of those who urge this and with the importance of the work itself, that I would be very glad indeed if we could organize some office or officers here who would be able to spread information through the country in regard to human medicine in the same way as we in my department distribute it to-day in regard to the health of animals and other agricultural matters. But I fear the difficulties and do not believe that it would be possible for us lightly or easily to overcome those difficulties. I would be glad to do it. I know that some of my colleagues at all events are in sympathy with me in this, but it is so important a question, so difficult a question, that I do not consider we would be justified at the present moment in adopting this resolution in a thin House on such a day as this, and I would1 therefore ask my friend to allow me
to adjourn the debate in order that we may have it more thoroughly threshed out and have the opinion and views of more members of the House and that the government can have an opportunity of seeing whether there is any possible way of accomplishing what is here aimed at. I beg therefore to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. FISHER moved the adjournment of the House.

Mr. Speaker, before the House adjourns I beg to call the attention of the government to the fact that two of the buoys or aids to navigation near the entrance to Yarmouth harbour, the northwest buoy and the southwest buoy, have been out of position for some time, the former for several days, and the latter for about three weeks. In this connection I may read a short extract from the Yarmouth ' Times ' of the 12th instant [DOT]
Officers of ships navigating the port of Yarmouth camplain bitterly to 'The Times' that two of the most important navigation aids off the harbour have been allowed to remain out of position for a long time. It is about three weeks since the south west buoy was found adrift and was towed into Abbott's Harbour, yet it appears that no effort has been made to replace it and this in spite of the fact that the department was promptly notified. Similarly the north west buoy was found adrift some days ago and towed into Yarmouth and although the 'Lansdowne' has been sent to restore it to its position and has been in port for some days nothing appears to have been accomplished. We are informed on good authority that the whole system of navigation aids along the coast is in a deranged condition. In the meantime lives and property are at a great risk and mariners are navigating their ships under a strain which they should not be called upon to bear. We repeat that a government steamer during the winter months should be constantly patrolling the coast between Yarmouth and Halifax.
Yarmouth is a very important port. Apart altogether from the large number of merchant vessels ordinarily visiting such a port there is a large fleet of fishing vessels which are constantly in and about that port. There are also the steamers of the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company which ply between that port and Boston, making several trips each way every week and carrying many passengers and valuable cargoes. The lack of proper aids to navigation may cause a serious loss not only of marine property but also of much more valuable life. The large expenditures which the Department of Marine is making in connection with the aids to navigation should, it seems to me,

assure the most ample protection which could be afforded. However that may be, it is incumbent upon the government to make the most ample provision for the proper maintenance of aids to navigation, not only in the Bay of Fundy, but also along the southwest shore of Nova Scotia, and anything short of such a provision, which will safeguard the lives and property of those interested, will leave the government responsible in the event M any disaster which may result from deficiency in these aids.
This matter now comes to my attention for the first time. I shall draw my colleague's attention to it, and I have no doubt the information required will be given.
What work will be taken up to-morrow?
First of all one or two minor Bills, then the resolution on the Civil Service, and then Supply, continuing the estimates of the Minister of the Interior.
